notes.title: Diabetic retinopathy: International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy (ICDR) grading
notes.sub: Five levels, the 4-2-1 rule, and what each grade means for review

blocks.p: Diabetic retinopathy is damage to the small retinal vessels from years of raised blood glucose. Capillaries leak, then close, and the retina becomes ischaemic (starved of blood). Late disease grows new vessels. The ICDR scale sorts an eye into five levels by the worst lesions present. Each level carries a different risk of progressing to proliferative disease. So the grade sets both the review interval and the urgency.

ul: **Microaneurysms** (small bulges in capillary walls): tiny, round, sharp-edged red dots. They are the earliest visible sign.
Dot and blot haemorrhages: larger, deeper red spots. Flame haemorrhages lie in the nerve fibre layer (the layer of ganglion cell axons).
Hard exudates: crisp yellow deposits of leaked lipid, often in rings around leaking vessels.
Cotton wool spots: pale fluffy patches. They are small infarcts (areas of tissue death from lost blood supply) of the nerve fibre layer.
Venous beading (veins that look like a string of beads) and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA): markers of significant ischaemia.

img.alt: Colour fundus photograph with only a few faint tiny red dots near the macula
img.caption: Graded mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR): microaneurysms only. They are tiny red dots, so zoom in. Lesions this small are easy to miss on a phone.

img.alt: Colour fundus photograph with clusters of yellow hard exudates temporal to the fovea
img.caption: Graded moderate NPDR: clusters of yellow hard exudates temporal to the fovea. More than microaneurysms alone, but short of the severe level. Exudates this close to the centre call for an optical coherence tomography (OCT) scan.

img.alt: Colour fundus photograph with many blot haemorrhages and yellow exudates at the macula
img.caption: Graded severe NPDR: numerous blot haemorrhages spread through the visible retina, with a plaque of hard exudates at the macula. No new vessels are seen in this field.

ul: No apparent retinopathy: no abnormalities.
Mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR): microaneurysms only.
Moderate NPDR: more than microaneurysms only, but less than severe NPDR.

Severe NPDR, the **4-2-1 rule**: no signs of proliferation, plus any one of these. More than 20 intraretinal haemorrhages in each of four quadrants; definite venous beading in two or more quadrants; or prominent IRMA in one or more quadrants.
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR): new vessels, or vitreous or preretinal haemorrhage.

blocks.p: Macular oedema is graded separately and can occur at any level. In practice optical coherence tomography (OCT) now decides whether oedema involves the centre.

This is a general guide from the American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) Preferred Practice Pattern. No or mild NPDR without macular oedema is reviewed yearly. Moderate NPDR without oedema is reviewed every 6 to 12 months. Severe NPDR is reviewed every 3 to 4 months under a retina service. There, panretinal laser may be considered, especially when follow-up is unreliable. PDR and centre-involving oedema need prompt retina referral. Screening programmes use their own grading mapped to referral pathways, so follow the local one. At every level, control of glucose, blood pressure and lipids slows progression.

blocks.pearl: Grade the worst lesion you can see, then remember what you cannot see. One 45-degree macula-centred photograph misses most of the periphery. Severe NPDR and early new vessels can hide there.

ul: Calling a vessel crossing or a pigment speck a microaneurysm. Microaneurysms are round, red and do not continue as a vessel.
Missing fine new vessels on the disc. Zoom in on the disc before settling on moderate or severe NPDR.
Forgetting the macula. Any grade can carry macular oedema that needs treatment on its own.
Grading a single field as if it were the whole eye.

notes.title: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
notes.sub: New vessels, bleeding and traction; panretinal laser or intravitreal injections

blocks.p: When retinal ischaemia (lack of blood supply) becomes widespread, the hypoxic (oxygen-starved) retina releases vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). New vessels then grow from the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE). They grow along the retinal surface and into the vitreous scaffold. These vessels are fragile and bleed, and the fibrous tissue that follows them contracts. Untreated, proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) leads to vitreous haemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment and neovascular glaucoma.

ul: NVD: fine, irregular vessel loops on the disc or within one disc diameter of it.
NVE: frond-like vessels elsewhere, usually along the arcades. They lie at the border between perfused and non-perfused retina.
Preretinal haemorrhage: blood trapped behind the hyaloid (the back face of the vitreous), often boat-shaped with a flat upper level. Vitreous haemorrhage blurs the whole view.
Fibrovascular tissue: white sheets at the disc or along the arcades that can pull on the retina.
New vessels on the iris or in the angle (where the trabecular meshwork drains aqueous): look before dilating, and measure the intraocular pressure.

img.alt: Colour fundus photograph with large dark haemorrhages temporal to the macula and pale spots near the upper arcade
img.caption: Graded PDR: large dense haemorrhages lie temporal to the macula, with pale cotton wool spots along the upper arcade.

img.alt: Colour fundus photograph with round pale laser scars and white fibrous tissue at the disc
img.caption: Treated PDR: round pale panretinal laser scars in the periphery. White fibrovascular tissue sits at the disc, with fine retinal folds from its traction.

img.label: proliferative diabetic retinopathy
img.alt: Ultra-widefield retinal image with widespread blot haemorrhages
img.caption: Ultra-widefield image of proliferative diabetic retinopathy: blot haemorrhages spread widely across the retina. They reach far beyond the area one 45-degree photograph records.

blocks.p: The International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy (ICDR) scale grades any new vessels, or any vitreous or preretinal haemorrhage, as PDR. The Diabetic Retinopathy Study defined **high-risk characteristics**: NVD of about a quarter to a third of the disc area or more; any NVD with vitreous or preretinal haemorrhage; or NVE of half a disc area or more with haemorrhage. Eyes with high-risk features face the greatest short-term risk of severe visual loss.

ul: Refer promptly to a retina service.
Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) treats the ischaemic peripheral retina so that new vessels regress. The Diabetic Retinopathy Study showed it reduced severe visual loss by at least half.

Intravitreal anti-VEGF is an alternative. In Diabetic Retinopathy Clinical Research (DRCR) Retina Network Protocol S, ranibizumab was non-inferior (no worse) to PRP. This held for vision at two years, with less peripheral field loss. But it needs reliable, regular visits. Patients lost to follow-up on injections alone can progress quickly.
Choose with the patient. Coexisting centre-involving oedema favours anti-VEGF; uncertain follow-up favours PRP.
Vitrectomy for vitreous haemorrhage that does not clear, and for tractional detachment involving or threatening the macula. Also for combined tractional and rhegmatogenous (retinal break) detachment.
Rapid tightening of glucose control can briefly worsen retinopathy. So advanced disease should be under eye review when treatment is intensified.

blocks.pearl: A boat-shaped haemorrhage with a flat top in a diabetic eye is PDR until proven otherwise. Look for its source at the disc and along the arcades.

ul: Mistaking intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) for NVE. IRMA lie within the retina and do not cross over major vessels. New vessels sit on the surface and often do.
Assuming an eye that is quiet on injections is cured. New vessels can regrow when treatment stops.
Missing a tractional detachment behind vitreous haemorrhage. Use B-scan ultrasound when the fundus cannot be seen.
Treating the eye and forgetting the kidneys, blood pressure and lipids.

notes.title: Diabetic macular oedema on optical coherence tomography (OCT)
notes.sub: Centre-involving or not, the OCT signs, and when to inject

blocks.p: Diabetic macular oedema (DME) is thickening of the macula from fluid that leaks through a damaged blood-retinal barrier. It can occur at any grade of retinopathy. It is the commonest cause of reduced vision in diabetes. OCT measures it, locates it and shows how it responds to treatment.

ul: Intraretinal cysts: round dark spaces, mostly in the inner nuclear and outer plexiform layers.
Increased central thickness and loss of the foveal pit.
Hyperreflective foci and hard exudates: bright dots or plaques that often cast shadows.
Subretinal fluid: a dark lens under the fovea in some eyes.
Disorganisation of the retinal inner layers (DRIL) and a broken ellipsoid zone (a photoreceptor band): both predict a poorer visual result.

img.label: DME
img.alt: OCT B-scan with dark intraretinal cysts and bright deposits casting shadows
img.caption: OCT B-scan, diabetic macular oedema: dark cysts sit in the middle layers of the retina beside the fovea. Clusters of bright exudates cast shadows down into the choroid.

img.label: DME
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a large central cyst replacing the foveal pit
img.caption: OCT B-scan, centre-involving oedema: a large central cyst has replaced the foveal pit, and smaller cysts extend to both sides. A bright cluster of exudate shadows the layers beneath it.

img.label: cystoid macular edema
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a tall central cyst and smaller surrounding cysts
img.caption: OCT B-scan of cystoid macular oedema from the case conference: a tall central cyst with smaller spaces around it. Cystoid oedema of any cause looks like this. So the fundus and history decide whether it is diabetic.

blocks.p: The International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy (ICDR) oedema scale grades DME by how close thickening and exudates come to the centre. Treatment decisions now rest on OCT: **centre-involving** DME affects the central subfield, the central 1 millimetre (mm). Non-centre-involving DME spares it. The older Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) term was clinically significant macular oedema. It was defined on examination and guided focal laser.

ul: Centre-involving DME with reduced vision: intravitreal anti-VEGF (anti-vascular endothelial growth factor) is first line. Diabetic Retinopathy Clinical Research (DRCR) network Protocol T compared aflibercept, bevacizumab and ranibizumab. All improved vision. Aflibercept did better at one year when starting vision was 20/50 or worse.
Centre-involving DME with good vision (20/25 or better): DRCR Protocol V found close observation a reasonable choice, starting anti-VEGF only if vision fell.

Steroid implants (dexamethasone or fluocinolone acetonide): second line, or for persistent oedema in pseudophakic eyes (eyes with an intraocular lens). Watch for raised intraocular pressure and cataract.
Focal laser: for leaking microaneurysms away from the centre, or as an adjunct.
Systemic: glucose, blood pressure, lipids and kidney function.

blocks.pearl: A thick macula is not always diabetic. Look for an epiretinal membrane, a vein occlusion or recent cataract surgery before calling it DME.

ul: Treating the thickness map instead of the eye. Always read the B-scans and relate them to vision.
Missing vitreomacular traction (vitreous pulling on the macula), which may need surgery rather than injections.
Ignoring exudates creeping towards the fovea before the oedema is centre-involving.
Starting a steroid implant in a patient with glaucoma or a known intraocular pressure response, without a monitoring plan.

notes.title: Reading a macular optical coherence tomography (OCT) scan
notes.sub: The normal layers, a reading order, and common artefacts

blocks.p: OCT builds a cross-section of the retina from light scattered back by each tissue layer. Its axial (depth) resolution is a few micrometres. A macular B-scan is one slice through the fovea. A volume scan stacks many slices to build a thickness map. Reflectivity, not colour, carries the information. Fibre layers and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) are bright; nuclear layers are dark.
The normal layers, named by the International Nomenclature for Optical Coherence Tomography consensus, from the vitreous down:

ul: Posterior hyaloid (the back face of the vitreous), sometimes seen as a thin line in the vitreous. Then the inner limiting membrane at the retinal surface.
Nerve fibre layer (ganglion cell axons; bright, thicker towards the disc). Ganglion cell layer (ganglion cell bodies; grey). Inner plexiform layer (synapses of bipolar and ganglion cells; bright).

Inner nuclear layer (bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cell bodies; dark). Outer plexiform layer (photoreceptor to bipolar synapses; bright). Outer nuclear layer (photoreceptor nuclei; dark, thickest at the fovea).
Four outer bands: external limiting membrane, **ellipsoid zone** (photoreceptor inner segments), interdigitation zone, and the RPE and Bruch's membrane complex.
Choroid below, then sclera.

blocks.p: At the fovea the inner layers slide aside and leave a smooth, symmetric pit.

img.label: NO
img.alt: OCT B-scan of a normal macula with a smooth central foveal pit
img.caption: OCT B-scan of a normal macula: a smooth, symmetric foveal pit, every layer continuous and a flat bright RPE band. The thin vertical dark stripes are shadows of retinal vessels.

img.label: NO
img.alt: Steeply curved OCT B-scan of a normal macula in a myopic eye
img.caption: Normal macula in a myopic eye: the scan curves steeply and the choroid is thin. Yet the layers are intact and there is no fluid.

ul: Check the scan: which eye, where the slice runs, and the signal strength.
Vitreous and surface: hyaloid attachment, traction, membranes.
Contour: is the pit present and symmetric; is the retina thick or thin?
Inner retina: cysts, bright foci, disorganisation, thinning.
Fluid: inside the retina or under it.
Outer retina: are the external limiting membrane and ellipsoid zone continuous?
RPE and choroid: bumps, detachments, atrophy with light passing into the choroid, choroidal thickness.

blocks.p: Compare every follow-up scan with the previous one at the same location. Most machines do this automatically. Use the thickness map to spot change, then confirm on the B-scans. Record what you see in layer terms: the shared vocabulary makes letters and referrals precise.

blocks.pearl: Never trust a thickness number alone. Automatic segmentation (the software's tracing of the layers) often fails on diseased retina. So scroll through the B-scans before you believe the map.

ul: Vessel shadows: vertical dark stripes under retinal vessels are not disease.
Off-centre scans: a slice that misses the fovea can fake a flat or absent pit.
Long eyes: steep curvature and a thin choroid are normal in myopia.
Weak signal from cataract, dry cornea or a blink can mimic loss of the outer bands.

sources: Staurenghi G, Sadda S, Chakravarthy U, Spaide RF; International Nomenclature for Optical Coherence Tomography (IN-OCT) Panel. Proposed lexicon for anatomic landmarks in normal posterior segment spectral-domain optical coherence tomography: the IN-OCT consensus. Ophthalmology 2014;121(8):1572-1578.
Huang D, Swanson EA, Lin CP, et al. Optical coherence tomography. Science 1991;254(5035):1178-1181.

notes.title: Dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD): drusen and atrophy
notes.sub: Beckman stages, optical coherence tomography risk signs, supplements, home tests

blocks.p: AMD is a degenerative disease of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), Bruch's membrane and choriocapillaris in people over 50. Bruch's membrane is the layer between the RPE and the choroid. The non-neovascular or "dry" form covers early and intermediate AMD. It also covers the late atrophic form, geographic atrophy (sharp-edged patches of RPE loss). It progresses slowly, but an eye can convert to neovascular AMD at any stage. Risk rises with age, smoking, family history and common genetic variants.

ul: Drusen: yellow deposits under the RPE; on optical coherence tomography (OCT), dome-shaped elevations of the RPE band.
Pigmentary change: clumps or loss of pigment; on OCT, bright foci in the retina above drusen, a sign of higher risk.
Reticular pseudodrusen (subretinal drusenoid deposits): these sit above the RPE and also carry high risk.
Drusenoid pigment epithelial detachment: large drusen merging into a broad dome.

Atrophy: loss of RPE and photoreceptors, so light passes deep into the choroid (hypertransmission). On OCT this is complete RPE and outer retinal atrophy (**cRORA**). This applies when the hypertransmission is at least 250 micrometres wide, with RPE loss and outer retinal thinning above it.

img.label: AMD
img.alt: OCT B-scan with small bumps in the RPE line under the fovea
img.caption: OCT B-scan, early AMD: small dome-shaped bumps of the RPE (drusen) under and beside the fovea. The retina above is dry and intact.

img.label: AMD
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a broad smooth dome lifting the RPE
img.caption: OCT B-scan, intermediate AMD: a broad dome lifts the RPE, filled with fairly uniform material. This is a drusenoid detachment formed by confluent large drusen. There is no fluid in or under the retina.

ul: No ageing changes: no drusen and no AMD pigment change.
Normal ageing: small drusen only, 63 micrometres or less.
Early AMD: medium drusen, over 63 and up to 125 micrometres, without pigment change.
Intermediate AMD: large drusen over 125 micrometres, or any AMD pigment change.
Late AMD: neovascular AMD or geographic atrophy.

blocks.p: A 125 micrometre druse is about the width of a major retinal vein at the disc margin. This makes a handy ruler at the slit lamp.

ul: Stop smoking: the strongest risk the patient can change.

Age-Related Eye Disease Study 2 (AREDS2) formula supplements for intermediate AMD, or for late AMD in one eye, lower the risk of progression. The formula uses lutein and zeaxanthin in place of beta-carotene. Beta-carotene raised lung cancer risk in smokers.
No supplement helps early AMD or reverses atrophy.
Home monitoring of each eye separately with an Amsler grid (a square grid that shows distortion) or similar. New distortion or blur needs review within days.

Geographic atrophy: complement inhibitor injections (pegcetacoplan, avacincaptad pegol) slowed lesion growth in trials without improving vision. Approval and availability vary by country. Offer low-vision rehabilitation.

blocks.pearl: The danger in dry AMD is conversion. Teach every patient with intermediate disease to test each eye alone and to report new distortion at once.

ul: Missing a small pocket of fluid in an eye labelled dry. Check every scan for intraretinal and subretinal fluid.
Calling a drusenoid detachment wet. Drusenoid ones have uniform, medium reflectivity and no fluid.
Labelling a pattern dystrophy or pachychoroid disease (a thick, congested choroid) in a younger patient as AMD.
Recommending beta-carotene formulas to smokers or former smokers.

notes.title: Neovascular age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and anti-VEGF (anti-vascular endothelial growth factor)
notes.sub: Spot the fluid, name the neovascularisation type, treat without delay

blocks.p: In neovascular (wet) AMD, new vessels grow from the choroid under or through the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). This is macular neovascularisation (MNV). The vessels leak fluid and blood. Untreated, they end in a fibrous disciform (disc-shaped) scar. Vision can fall within weeks, so this is the time-critical form of AMD. Typical symptoms are new distortion, a central blur or grey patch. These are often noticed only when the other eye is covered.

ul: Subretinal fluid: a dark space between the neurosensory retina and the RPE.
Intraretinal fluid: cysts within the retina; it tends to harm vision more.
Pigment epithelial detachment (PED): serous (dark dome), fibrovascular (irregular, mixed reflectivity) or haemorrhagic.
Subretinal hyperreflective material: blood, fibrin or neovascular tissue above the RPE.
On the fundus: a grey-green membrane, haemorrhage or exudate at the macula.

img.alt: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) B-scan with a dark pocket of fluid under the retina
img.caption: OCT B-scan, neovascular AMD: a dark pocket of subretinal fluid lifts the neurosensory retina off the RPE.

img.label: AMD
img.alt: OCT B-scan with intraretinal cysts over a broad bright elevation of the RPE
img.caption: OCT B-scan, neovascular AMD: intraretinal cysts sit above a broad elevation of the RPE. It is filled with bright, mixed material, the appearance of an active fibrovascular lesion.

img.label: polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a steep, sharp-peaked dome under the retina
img.caption: OCT B-scan from the case conference labelled polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy: a steep, sharp-peaked pigment epithelial detachment. Indocyanine green angiography confirms the polyps.

blocks.h: Classification (2020 Consensus on Neovascular AMD Nomenclature, CONAN)

ul: Type 1 MNV: under the RPE, the old "occult" pattern. Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (polyp-like dilations of choroidal vessels) is a variant, common in Asian patients. It has sharp-peaked PEDs and polyps on indocyanine green angiography.
Type 2 MNV: above the RPE in the subretinal space, the old "classic" pattern.
Type 3 MNV: arising from the deep retinal capillaries, formerly retinal angiomatous proliferation.
Refer urgently to a macular service; every week of delay costs vision.

Intravitreal anti-VEGF is standard care. MARINA (Minimally Classic/Occult Trial of the Anti-VEGF Antibody Ranibizumab in the Treatment of Neovascular AMD): monthly ranibizumab held or improved vision. Sham-treated eyes lost vision. CATT (Comparison of Age-related Macular Degeneration Treatments Trials) found bevacizumab and ranibizumab equivalent for vision at one year. Aflibercept and newer agents, such as faricimab and brolucizumab, widen the choice.
Treatment starts with monthly loading injections, then the interval is adjusted to activity. Commonly this is **treat-and-extend**: extend when the macula is dry, shorten when fluid returns.
Polypoidal disease: anti-VEGF, with photodynamic therapy (verteporfin activated by laser light) as an option guided by indocyanine green angiography.
Most patients need injections for years. The fellow eye is at high risk, so teach home monitoring.

blocks.pearl: Fluid is the activity signal. At every visit ask whether intraretinal or subretinal fluid is new or larger. Let that answer set the next interval.

ul: Injecting a drusenoid detachment or dry atrophy as if it were active disease.
Missing polypoidal disease in an eye with a sharp-peaked PED that responds poorly: arrange indocyanine green angiography.
Calling central serous chorioretinopathy wet AMD in a younger patient with a thick choroid.
Delaying review of pain, redness or falling vision after an injection: endophthalmitis (infection inside the eye) needs same-day assessment.

notes.title: Retinal vein occlusion
notes.sub: Branch or central, ischaemic or not, and the 90-day danger

blocks.p: A thrombus (clot) blocks a retinal vein. A branch vein can block at an arteriovenous crossing: branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO). The central vein can block at or behind the lamina cribrosa (the sieve-like plate where the optic nerve exits). This is central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). Venous pressure rises, blood and fluid leak, and capillaries may close. After diabetic retinopathy it is the commonest retinal vascular disease. Risk factors are age, hypertension, diabetes, raised lipids and smoking. Raised intraocular pressure or glaucoma is also a risk factor, especially for CRVO.

ul: CRVO: haemorrhages in all four quadrants, dilated tortuous veins, disc swelling and cotton wool spots.

BRVO: a wedge of flame haemorrhages drained by one vein, with its apex at a crossing. It respects the horizontal raphe (the horizontal dividing line of the retina). The superotemporal branch is most often affected.
Optical coherence tomography (OCT): cystoid macular oedema, often with subretinal fluid and inner retinal thickening.
Ischaemia: many cotton wool spots, poor vision and a relative afferent pupillary defect (weaker pupil reaction to light in that eye). Wide capillary non-perfusion shows on fluorescein angiography.

img.label: central retinal vein occlusion
img.alt: Ultra-widefield image with haemorrhages radiating from the disc into all quadrants
img.caption: Ultra-widefield image of a central retinal vein occlusion: flame and blot haemorrhages radiate from the disc into all four quadrants. The veins are engorged and tortuous.

img.label: branch retinal vein occlusion
img.alt: Fundus photograph with flame haemorrhages and white spots in the upper temporal retina
img.caption: Fundus photograph of a branch retinal vein occlusion: feathery flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots fill the superotemporal sector. One vein drains this sector; the lower retina is spared.

img.label: RVO
img.alt: OCT B-scan with large cysts in the retina and fluid beneath it
img.caption: OCT B-scan, vein occlusion with macular oedema: large intraretinal cysts thicken the retina. A pocket of subretinal fluid lies beneath them.

blocks.p: The key division is **non-ischaemic versus ischaemic**. The Central Vein Occlusion Study defined ischaemic CRVO as 10 or more disc areas of non-perfusion on angiography. Ischaemic CRVO risks new vessels on the iris and in the angle (where the trabecular meshwork drains aqueous). This classically happens within the first three months, hence "90-day glaucoma". Some non-ischaemic eyes convert later.

ul: Macular oedema: intravitreal anti-VEGF (anti-vascular endothelial growth factor) is first line for both BRVO and CRVO. A dexamethasone implant is an alternative. Grid laser still has a place for persistent oedema after BRVO.

New vessels: panretinal laser to the ischaemic retina once neovascularisation appears. In the Central Vein Occlusion Study, prophylactic laser did not reliably prevent it. So close follow-up is the safeguard.
In ischaemic CRVO, examine the iris and angle at each visit in the first months. Do gonioscopy (viewing the angle through a mirrored contact lens) before dilating.

Systemic work-up: blood pressure, glucose, lipids, full blood count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and intraocular pressure in both eyes. Reserve thrombophilia (clotting tendency) or inflammatory tests for young, bilateral or atypical cases.
Share care with the family doctor: a vein occlusion is a marker of cardiovascular risk.

blocks.pearl: In every vein occlusion, measure the intraocular pressure in both eyes. Glaucoma and raised pressure are treatable risk factors, especially for CRVO.

ul: Mid-peripheral blot haemorrhages with dilated but not tortuous veins in an older patient may not be CRVO. They may be ocular ischaemic syndrome from carotid artery disease.
Bilateral CRVO-like changes suggest hyperviscosity (thickened blood) or a blood disorder.
Discharging a non-ischaemic CRVO too early: some convert to ischaemic within months.
Dilating the pupil before looking for new vessels on the iris.

notes.title: Retinal artery occlusion: an eye stroke
notes.sub: Sudden painless loss, same-day stroke work-up, think of giant cell arteritis

blocks.p: An embolus (travelling clot or debris) or a thrombus blocks the central retinal artery or one of its branches. The central retinal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery and supplies the inner retina. The blocks are central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) and branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO). The inner retina, which depends on the retinal circulation, becomes ischaemic (starved of blood) within minutes to hours. Most emboli come from the carotid artery or the heart. In anyone over 50, giant cell arteritis (GCA) must be excluded. A retinal artery occlusion is a stroke of the retina. These patients carry a high short-term risk of cerebral stroke.

ul: Sudden, painless, profound loss of vision in that eye in CRAO. In BRAO, field loss in the sector the blocked branch supplies. CRAO usually gives a relative afferent pupillary defect (weaker pupil reaction to light in that eye).
Retinal whitening from inner retinal oedema, with a **cherry-red spot** at the fovea. There the thin retina lets the choroid show through.
Narrowed arteries and a segmented blood column in severe cases.
Emboli: bright, refractile cholesterol plaques at bifurcations, or white calcific or grey platelet emboli.
A cilioretinal artery (fed by the short posterior ciliary circulation) can spare a tongue of retina between disc and fovea. It can preserve central vision.
Optical coherence tomography (OCT), acute: thickened, bright inner retina that shadows the outer layers. Later, inner retinal thinning.

img.label: RAO
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a thick, bright inner retina shadowing the layers beneath
img.caption: OCT B-scan, acute retinal artery occlusion: the inner retina is thickened and bright and shadows the outer layers. The outer retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) keep their shape because the choroid still supplies them.

img.label: branch retinal artery occlusion
img.alt: Ultra-widefield false-colour image with a pale hazy area above the temporal arcade
img.caption: Ultra-widefield image labelled branch retinal artery occlusion: the retina above the temporal arcade looks pale and hazy. A narrowed branch artery supplies it. Whitening is harder to judge on these false colours than on a colour photograph.

blocks.p: Hayreh separated CRAO into non-arteritic permanent, non-arteritic transient, non-arteritic with cilioretinal sparing, and arteritic (from inflamed arteries). The arteritic form, from GCA, threatens the other eye within days.

ul: Same day: send the patient to a stroke service or emergency department for vascular work-up: brain imaging, carotid imaging, heart rhythm monitoring, blood pressure, glucose and lipids.

Over 50: erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP) and a full blood count at once. If GCA is suspected, start high-dose steroids the same day, without waiting for biopsy. Clues are headache, jaw claudication (jaw pain on chewing), scalp tenderness and raised markers.

No ocular treatment is proven. Ocular massage, paracentesis (removing fluid from the anterior chamber) and pressure lowering have not shown benefit. The European Assessment Group for Lysis in the Eye (EAGLE) trial found local intra-arterial fibrinolysis no better than conservative care. It also had more adverse events. Intravenous thrombolysis early after onset is under study. Some stroke services offer it within a protocol.
Review for new vessels on the iris and angle in the weeks to months after CRAO.

blocks.pearl: The retina is brain tissue. A retinal artery occlusion needs the same urgent vascular work-up as a stroke. Anyone over 50 needs an ESR and CRP that day.

ul: Booking a routine clinic next week: stroke risk is highest in the first days.
Ruling out GCA because there is no headache: it can present with vision loss alone.
Missing a BRAO when the patient reports only a patch of missing vision. Look for whitening along one arteriole and an embolus.
Forgetting the fellow eye and the heart: check for atrial fibrillation.

sources: Mac Grory B, Schrag M, Biousse V, et al. Management of central retinal artery occlusion: a scientific statement from the American Heart Association. Stroke 2021;52(6):e282-e294.

Schumacher M, Schmidt D, Jurklies B, et al; EAGLE-Study Group. Central retinal artery occlusion: local intra-arterial fibrinolysis versus conservative treatment, a multicenter randomized trial. Ophthalmology 2010;117(7):1367-1375.

Kovach JL, Bailey ST, Kim SJ, et al. Retinal and Ophthalmic Artery Occlusions Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2025;132(4):P270-P302.

notes.title: Epiretinal membrane
notes.sub: A sheet on the retina: optical coherence tomography stages and when to peel

blocks.p: An epiretinal membrane (ERM) is a thin fibrocellular sheet that grows on the inner surface of the macula. It contracts, wrinkling and thickening the retina. Most are idiopathic (no known cause) and follow posterior vitreous detachment (vitreous gel separating from the retina) in older people. Secondary membranes follow retinal tears and detachment surgery, vein occlusion, diabetic retinopathy, uveitis or trauma. Many cause no symptoms. Others cause distortion, blur, or a size difference between the two eyes' images.

ul: Fundus: a cellophane sheen early; later a grey-white membrane with radiating retinal folds and straightened or tortuous vessels.
Optical coherence tomography (OCT): a bright line on the retinal surface, sometimes lifted off in places.
Flattening or loss of the foveal pit, with diffuse thickening. Some eyes show steep foveal walls, a pseudohole (it looks like a hole but is not one).
**Ectopic inner foveal layers**: a continuous band of inner retina running across the centre of the fovea. It is a sign of longstanding traction.
Cystoid spaces in some eyes.

img.label: ERM
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a thin bright membrane on the retinal surface, partly lifted
img.caption: OCT B-scan of an epiretinal membrane: a thin bright line lies on the retinal surface and lifts off it in places. The inner retina is thickened and wrinkled, and the foveal pit is narrowed.

img.label: epiretinal membrane
img.alt: OCT B-scan with an irregular bright surface layer and a thick retina without a foveal pit
img.caption: OCT B-scan of an epiretinal membrane: an irregular bright layer covers the retinal surface. The retina beneath is diffusely thickened, and the foveal pit has gone.

ul: Stage 1: foveal pit present, layers clearly defined.
Stage 2: pit lost and outer nuclear layer widened, layers still defined.
Stage 3: continuous ectopic inner foveal layers across the fovea, layers still identifiable.
Stage 4: ectopic inner foveal layers with disorganised, unidentifiable layers.

blocks.p: Higher stages were linked with worse vision before and after surgery.

ul: Observe when symptoms are mild. Recheck vision and distortion, with OCT if symptoms change. Many membranes stay stable.

Surgery: pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peel, often with internal limiting membrane peel. The internal limiting membrane is the basement membrane of the Muller cells on the retinal surface. Surgery is done when distortion or vision loss affects daily life.
Recovery is gradual over months, and distortion may not fully resolve. Cataract usually progresses after vitrectomy in eyes with their own lens.
For secondary membranes, treat the cause as well.

blocks.pearl: Operate on symptoms, not on the scan. Ectopic inner foveal layers predict a less complete recovery, so they belong in the consent discussion.

ul: Missing a lamellar or full-thickness hole under the membrane: scroll through every B-scan.
Blaming the membrane for poor vision caused by cataract, age-related macular degeneration or amblyopia.
Missing a peripheral retinal tear behind a secondary membrane: examine the periphery.
Calling the normal bright surface reflex of a young retina a membrane.

sources: Govetto A, Lalane RA 3rd, Sarraf D, Figueroa MS, Hubschman JP. Insights into epiretinal membranes: presence of ectopic inner foveal layers and a new optical coherence tomography staging scheme. Am J Ophthalmol 2017;175:99-113.
Bailey ST, Vemulakonda GA, Kim SJ, et al. Idiopathic Epiretinal Membrane and Vitreomacular Traction Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2025;132(4):P197-P233.
Duker JS, Kaiser PK, Binder S, et al. The International Vitreomacular Traction Study Group classification of vitreomacular adhesion, traction, and macular hole. Ophthalmology 2013;120(12):2611-2619.

notes.title: Macular hole and vitreomacular traction
notes.sub: International Vitreomacular Traction Study terms, hole size, vitrectomy and peel

blocks.p: As the vitreous separates from the retina with age, it can stay stuck at the fovea. When it pulls and distorts the fovea, this is vitreomacular traction (VMT). When the pull opens the fovea through its full thickness, it is a full-thickness macular hole (FTMH). The typical patient is a woman in her sixties or seventies with central blur and distortion. Holes also follow trauma and occur in high myopia.

ul: Symptoms: central blur, distortion, a small central gap; straight lines look pinched at the centre.
Fundus: a round red defect at the fovea, often with a grey cuff of fluid; a small operculum (a detached plug of tissue) may float in front.
Slit beam test: a thin beam across a full-thickness hole looks broken to the patient.
Optical coherence tomography (OCT), VMT: hyaloid attached at the fovea, which is distorted or holds pseudocysts.
OCT, FTMH: a defect through every neural layer down to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), with cystic edges.
OCT, lamellar hole: an irregular inner defect with the outer retina intact.

img.label: VID
img.alt: OCT B-scan with the vitreous detached on both sides but still attached at the fovea
img.caption: OCT B-scan, vitreomacular traction: the posterior hyaloid has come away from the retina on both sides. It stays attached at the fovea and pulls it upward.

img.label: VID
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a full-thickness gap at the fovea and a vitreous strand attached to its edge
img.caption: OCT B-scan, full-thickness macular hole: a gap through every neural layer down to the RPE, with small cysts in its edges. The hyaloid is still tethered to a flap at the rim.

img.label: VID
img.alt: OCT B-scan with an irregular inner foveal defect and an intact outer retina
img.caption: OCT B-scan, lamellar macular hole: an irregular defect in the inner fovea, with a split between inner and outer retina. The outer retina beneath stays intact.

ul: Vitreomacular adhesion: vitreous separated around the fovea but still attached at it, with no retinal change.
Vitreomacular traction: attachment with foveal distortion; focal if 1500 micrometres or less, broad if wider.
Full-thickness macular hole, sized by the narrowest width: small 250 micrometres or less, medium over 250 up to 400, large over 400; with or without VMT; primary or secondary.
Lamellar hole and pseudohole are separate diagnoses.
Adhesion alone: no treatment.
VMT: observe when mild, as many release on their own; vitrectomy when symptoms are significant or progressing.

FTMH: pars plana vitrectomy, internal limiting membrane (ILM) peel and gas tamponade (an internal gas bubble), plus posturing as the surgeon advises. The gas is usually sulphur hexafluoride or perfluoropropane. Small and medium holes close in most eyes. Large or longstanding holes close less often. An inverted ILM flap is one option for them.
Lamellar hole: usually observed; surgery if vision falls.
Cataract usually follows vitrectomy in eyes with their own lens.

blocks.pearl: Measure a macular hole at its narrowest point, not at its base. That width predicts closure and guides the choice of technique.

ul: Calling a pseudohole a hole. In a pseudohole from a membrane, the outer retina is intact.
Missing an impending hole: a foveal pseudocyst under traction can progress.
Delaying referral: larger and older holes close less often and recover less vision.
Forgetting the fellow eye, which may show adhesion or traction.

sources: Duker JS, Kaiser PK, Binder S, et al. The International Vitreomacular Traction Study Group classification of vitreomacular adhesion, traction, and macular hole. Ophthalmology 2013;120(12):2611-2619.
Gass JD. Reappraisal of biomicroscopic classification of stages of development of a macular hole. Am J Ophthalmol 1995;119(6):752-759.
Michalewska Z, Michalewski J, Adelman RA, Nawrocki J. Inverted internal limiting membrane flap technique for large macular holes. Ophthalmology 2010;117(10):2018-2025.
Kim SJ, Lim JI, Bailey ST, et al. Idiopathic Macular Hole Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2025;132(4):P234-P269.

notes.title: Retinal detachment: rhegmatogenous, tractional, exudative
notes.sub: Three mechanisms, how to tell them apart, how urgent repair is

blocks.p: A retinal detachment is fluid between the neurosensory retina and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Once separated, the photoreceptors lose their blood supply from the choriocapillaris and start to die. So time matters. There are three ways fluid gets there, and each needs a different treatment.

ul: **Rhegmatogenous**: a full-thickness break lets liquefied vitreous pass under the retina. It is the commonest type. It usually follows a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) that tears the retina.

**Tractional**: fibrovascular or fibrous membranes pull the retina off without a break. This happens in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, vein occlusion, retinopathy of prematurity or penetrating trauma.

**Exudative (serous)**: fluid leaks from choroid or retinal vessels with no break and no traction. Causes are tumours, posterior scleritis, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease, Coats disease, severe hypertension or pre-eclampsia.

blocks.p: Ask about flashes, a shower of new floaters and a curtain or shadow in the field. After an acute PVD, anterior vitreous pigment cells (Shafer sign, tobacco dust) or vitreous haemorrhage make a retinal tear likely: examine the whole periphery dilated, with scleral depression (indenting the eye wall to see the far periphery).

img.label: rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
img.alt: Widefield image of a corrugated detached retina with a large superotemporal break
img.caption: Widefield scanning laser ophthalmoscope image: a grey, corrugated detached retina over three quadrants reaching the macula. A large retinal break lies superotemporally. This is a rhegmatogenous detachment.

img.label: tractional retinal detachment
img.alt: Fundus photo with fibrous proliferation around the disc, retinal folds and old pigment
img.caption: Colour fundus photograph: fibrous tissue around the disc with folds of retina drawn towards it and scattered old pigment. This is the appearance of a chronic tractional detachment.

ul: Rhegmatogenous: convex, corrugated, moves with eye movement, usually extends to the ora serrata (the front edge of the retina). A break can be found.
Tractional: concave, taut, immobile, rarely reaches the ora, membranes visible.
Exudative: smooth and convex, fluid shifts to the lowest part when the patient changes posture. No break, and a cause to find.

img.label: retinal detachment
img.alt: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) B-scan showing the retina lifted off the RPE by dark fluid under the macula
img.caption: OCT B-scan: the neurosensory retina is lifted off the RPE by optically empty subretinal fluid involving the macula. OCT confirms the macula is off but does not show the mechanism.

img.label: retinal detachment
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with a bright curved membrane in the posterior vitreous cavity
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: a bright, curved membrane in the posterior eye, the echo of detached retina. Ultrasound finds a detachment when blood or cataract hides the fundus.

blocks.p: Treat symptomatic horseshoe tears with laser or cryotherapy (freezing treatment) before they detach. A rhegmatogenous detachment with the macula still attached is an emergency. Refer the same day, because once the fovea detaches the final acuity falls. Repair closes every break by one of three routes. The route is chosen on the break position, lens status and complexity:

ul: Pneumatic retinopexy: a gas bubble plus cryotherapy or laser, for a single break in the upper retina. In eyes eligible for both, it gave better vision than vitrectomy. This was shown in PIVOT (Pneumatic Retinopexy versus Vitrectomy for the Management of Primary Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment Outcomes Randomized Trial).
Scleral buckle (a band sewn onto the eye wall): often preferred in young phakic eyes (with their own lens) and retinal dialysis (a tear at the ora).
Vitrectomy with gas or silicone oil: most pseudophakic, complex or proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) cases.
Tractional detachment: vitrectomy when the macula is involved or threatened. Exudative detachment: treat the cause, not the fluid.

blocks.pearl: Flashes and floaters with pigment in the vitreous mean a tear until the whole periphery has been examined.

ul: Reassuring a patient with PVD symptoms without a dilated peripheral examination.
Treating an exudative detachment surgically: shifting fluid and no break point to a medical cause.
Forgetting to re-examine after an uncomplicated PVD; new symptoms need review the same day.
Calling a PVD on ultrasound a detachment: a detached retina is thicker, brighter and stays attached at the disc.

sources: Kim SJ, Bailey ST, Kovach JL, et al. Posterior Vitreous Detachment, Retinal Breaks, and Lattice Degeneration Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2025;132(4):P163-P196.

Hillier RJ, Felfeli T, Berger AR, et al. The Pneumatic Retinopexy versus Vitrectomy for the Management of Primary Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment Outcomes Randomized Trial (PIVOT). Ophthalmology 2019;126(4):531-539.
Hollands H, Johnson D, Brox AC, et al. Acute-onset floaters and flashes: is this patient at risk for retinal detachment? JAMA 2009;302(20):2243-2249.

notes.title: Central serous chorioretinopathy
notes.sub: Serous macular detachment, the steroid link, when to treat

blocks.p: Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC) is a serous detachment of the neurosensory retina at the macula. A thick, hyperpermeable (leaky) choroid pushes fluid through a weak point in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). This is part of the pachychoroid (thick choroid) spectrum. CSC typically affects adults aged 20 to 50, more often men. It is often bilateral on imaging even when only one eye has symptoms.

Symptoms are blurred or dim central vision, distortion, objects looking smaller (micropsia) and a hyperopic shift (refraction becomes more plus). Acuity is often only mildly reduced and may improve with a plus lens. Risk factors to ask about: **corticosteroids by any route** (tablets, inhalers, nasal sprays, skin creams, joint injections), Cushing syndrome, pregnancy and psychological stress.

img.label: central serous chorioretinopathy
img.alt: Widefield retinal image with a round blister-like elevation at the macula
img.caption: Widefield scanning laser ophthalmoscope image: a round, well-defined serous elevation at the macula without haemorrhage.

img.label: central serous chorioretinopathy
img.alt: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) B-scan with a dome of dark fluid under the fovea
img.caption: OCT B-scan: a dome of optically empty subretinal fluid lifts the fovea; the inner retina keeps its layers and there is no intraretinal cyst.

ul: Optical coherence tomography (OCT): subretinal fluid, often with a small pigment epithelial detachment at the leak. Longer-standing fluid shows elongated photoreceptor tips. A thick choroid shows on enhanced-depth or swept-source OCT.
Fluorescein angiography: one or a few leaks, usually an expanding ink blot. Less often a smokestack rises through the fluid.
Chronic disease: widespread RPE changes, gravitational tracts (downward streaks) of atrophy, less fluid but worse vision.
Indocyanine green angiography shows choroidal hyperpermeability. It helps exclude polypoidal vasculopathy or neovascularisation.

img.label: central serous chorioretinopathy
img.alt: Series of fluorescein angiogram frames with a bright spot that grows over time
img.caption: Fluorescein angiogram frames, early to late: a focal hyperfluorescent point near the inferotemporal arcade enlarges as dye leaks. This is the ink-blot pattern of CSC.

blocks.p: Traditionally acute (recent, usually self-limiting) or chronic (persistent fluid or widespread RPE change). A multimodal-imaging consensus now sorts eyes into simple and complex CSC, with or without persistent fluid and atrophy.

ul: Stop or reduce corticosteroids where medically safe, with the prescribing doctor. Never stop systemic steroids abruptly.
Acute CSC: observe; most eyes dry within a few months.

Persistent or chronic CSC: half-dose or half-fluence (half light dose) photodynamic therapy with verteporfin. In PLACE (the trial of half-dose photodynamic therapy versus high-density subthreshold micropulse laser), it beat micropulse laser.
Eplerenone was no better than placebo in VICI (the trial of eplerenone in chronic CSC). So mineralocorticoid antagonists such as eplerenone and spironolactone are not routine.
Anti-VEGF (anti-vascular endothelial growth factor) only if secondary choroidal neovascularisation develops.
Review until the macula is dry. Recurrences are common and each one costs photoreceptors.

blocks.pearl: Ask every patient with CSC about every steroid: creams, inhalers and joint injections are easily forgotten.

ul: Calling subretinal fluid in an older patient CSC without excluding neovascular age-related macular degeneration or polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy.
Treating with corticosteroids, which makes CSC worse.
Missing bilateral serous detachments from Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease or an optic disc pit.
Taking good acuity as reassurance: the distortion and reduced contrast can still limit work, and an Amsler grid shows it.

sources: van Dijk EHC, Fauser S, Breukink MB, et al. Half-dose photodynamic therapy versus high-density subthreshold micropulse laser treatment in patients with chronic central serous chorioretinopathy: the PLACE trial. Ophthalmology 2018;125(10):1547-1555.

Lotery A, Sivaprasad S, O'Connell A, et al. Eplerenone for chronic central serous chorioretinopathy in patients with active, previously untreated disease for more than 4 months (VICI): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet 2020;395(10220):294-303.
Chhablani J, Cohen FB; Central Serous Chorioretinopathy International Group. Multimodal imaging-based central serous chorioretinopathy classification. Ophthalmol Retina 2020;4(11):1043-1046.
Daruich A, Matet A, Dirani A, et al. Central serous chorioretinopathy: recent findings and new physiopathology hypothesis. Prog Retin Eye Res 2015;48:82-118.

notes.title: Choroidal melanoma and pigmented fundus lesions
notes.sub: Naevus or melanoma: the risk signs, ultrasound, referral

blocks.p: Choroidal melanoma is the commonest primary malignant tumour inside the adult eye. It arises from choroidal melanocytes (pigment cells), often from a pre-existing naevus (a benign pigmented lesion). It spreads by the blood, mainly to the liver. Choroidal naevi are common and nearly all stay benign. So the clinical skill is recognising the few pigmented lesions that are, or are becoming, melanoma.

img.label: choroidal melanoma
img.alt: Fundus photo with a dark, well-defined lesion at the macula with mottled surface
img.caption: Colour fundus photograph: a dark, well-defined lesion at the macula with mottled pigment on its surface. The dataset diagnosis is choroidal melanoma.

blocks.p: Shields and colleagues summarised the risk factors for growth of a small melanocytic lesion in a mnemonic. It reads To Find Small Ocular Melanoma Using Helpful Hints Daily:

ul: **T**hickness over 2 millimetres (mm); subretinal **F**luid; **S**ymptoms such as flashes or blurred vision.
**O**range pigment (lipofuscin) on the surface; **M**argin within 3 mm of the disc.
**U**ltrasonographic **H**ollowness; **H**alo (a pale ring around the lesion) absent; **D**rusen absent (drusen suggest a long-standing, quiet lesion).
The MOLES (mushroom shape, orange pigment, large size, enlargement, subretinal fluid) score (United Kingdom) is a simpler triage aid.

blocks.p: On ultrasound the mass is dome-shaped, or mushroom (collar-stud) shaped once it breaks through Bruch's membrane. Bruch's membrane is the layer between the retinal pigment epithelium and the choroid. The mass has low to medium internal reflectivity, acoustic hollowness (a dark interior) and sometimes choroidal excavation. It may cause a serous retinal detachment.

Look-alikes: congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE), which is flat, sharp-edged, often with pale lacunae. Choroidal haemangioma is orange-red, not pigmented. Metastasis is usually amelanotic (non-pigmented), sometimes multiple. Melanocytoma is a dark lesion on the disc. Blood under the retinal pigment epithelium can come from polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy.

img.label: solid intraocular mass
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with a large solid mass in the vitreous cavity and a curved retinal echo
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: a solid mass filling about half the vitreous cavity, with a bright internal focus casting an acoustic shadow. There is also a curved echo of detached retina. The dataset calls it a solid intraocular mass with retinal detachment. The scan alone does not name the tumour type.

ul: Photograph and measure every pigmented lesion; compare with old images.
Refer lesions with risk factors, documented growth or diagnostic doubt to an ocular oncology service. Low-risk naevi are monitored.

Treatment is chosen by size and position: plaque brachytherapy (a radioactive plaque sewn onto the sclera), proton beam radiotherapy, local resection or enucleation (removal of the eye). The Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study (COMS) trial found no survival difference between iodine-125 brachytherapy and enucleation for medium tumours.
Systemic staging and long-term liver surveillance. Tumour cytogenetics (for example monosomy 3) refine the metastatic risk.

blocks.pearl: A pigmented choroidal lesion with orange pigment, subretinal fluid or thickness over 2 mm needs an oncology opinion. Routine review is not enough.

ul: Labelling a lesion a naevus from one look without a baseline photograph.
Missing an amelanotic melanoma, or a metastasis, because it is not pigmented.
Mistaking a peripheral haemorrhage, CHRPE or melanocytoma for melanoma, or the reverse.
Biopsy or vitrectomy in an eye with an undiagnosed mass before an oncology opinion.

sources: Shields CL, Furuta M, Berman EL, et al. Choroidal nevus transformation into melanoma: analysis of 2514 consecutive cases. Arch Ophthalmol 2009;127(8):981-987.

Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study Group. The COMS randomized trial of iodine 125 brachytherapy for choroidal melanoma: V. Twelve-year mortality rates and prognostic factors: COMS report No. 28. Arch Ophthalmol 2006;124(12):1684-1693.

Kaliki S, Shields CL. Uveal melanoma: relatively rare but deadly cancer. Eye 2017;31(2):241-257.

notes.title: Pathological myopia
notes.sub: International Myopia Institute definitions, maculopathy grading, complications

blocks.p: The International Myopia Institute (IMI) defines myopia as a spherical equivalent of -0.50 dioptres (D) or more myopic, with accommodation relaxed. High myopia is -6.00 D or more myopic. Pathological myopia is different: excessive axial elongation (the eye grows too long) with structural damage to the back of the eye. This damage includes myopic maculopathy, staphyloma and optic nerve changes, and can reduce best-corrected vision. It is a leading cause of visual impairment in East Asia and increasingly worldwide.

img.label: high myopia
img.alt: Fundus photo with prominent choroidal vessels and a large pale zone of atrophy around the disc
img.caption: Colour fundus photograph: a tessellated (tigroid) fundus in which choroidal vessels show through thin retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). A wide zone of peripapillary atrophy surrounds the disc.

img.label: pathologic myopia
img.alt: Widefield retinal image of a tilted disc with peripapillary atrophy
img.caption: Widefield scanning laser ophthalmoscope image: a tilted disc with marked peripapillary atrophy of RPE and choroid in pathological myopia.

ul: Disc: tilted and oval, with a temporal crescent or wide ring of peripapillary atrophy.
Fundus: tessellation, then diffuse and patchy chorioretinal atrophy.
Lacquer cracks (yellow linear breaks in Bruch's membrane, under the RPE), myopic choroidal neovascularisation (CNV) and a pigmented Fuchs spot.
Posterior staphyloma: an outpouching of the eye wall, seen on optical coherence tomography (OCT) and ultrasound.

img.label: myopic foveoschisis
img.alt: OCT B-scan of a deeply curved macula with the retina split into layers
img.caption: OCT B-scan: the steeply curved contour of a staphyloma. The outer retina is split by columns and cavities (foveoschisis).

img.label: posterior scleral staphyloma
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound showing the back wall of the eye bulging outward
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: the posterior eye wall bulges outward in a localised protrusion, a posterior staphyloma in a highly myopic eye.

blocks.p: The Meta-analysis for Pathologic Myopia study group classification grades myopic maculopathy in five categories: 0 no lesion, 1 tessellated fundus, 2 diffuse chorioretinal atrophy, 3 patchy chorioretinal atrophy, 4 macular atrophy. Three plus lesions are recorded separately: lacquer cracks, myopic CNV and Fuchs spot. Category 2 or worse, any plus lesion or a staphyloma counts as pathological myopia.

ul: Sudden distortion or a new central blur: OCT the same week for myopic CNV. It usually responds to a few anti-VEGF (anti-vascular endothelial growth factor) injections.
Myopic traction maculopathy (foveoschisis, lamellar hole, foveal detachment): observe while stable; vitrectomy if vision falls or the fovea detaches.
Examine the periphery: lattice degeneration (thin, weak areas of peripheral retina) and retinal detachment are more common.
Teach warning symptoms: flashes, new floaters, a shadow or new distortion need review within days.

Children: more time outdoors delays onset. Low-dose atropine, myopia-control spectacle lenses, orthokeratology (overnight rigid lenses that reshape the cornea) or specific soft contact lenses slow progression. Follow current national guidance.

blocks.pearl: In a high myope, glaucoma is easy to miss. The tilted disc and peripapillary atrophy hide cupping, so rely on fields and OCT trends.

ul: Assuming poor vision is just the refraction and missing CNV or foveoschisis.
Reading a thin, myopic OCT against a normal database and calling it glaucoma, or the reverse.
Forgetting that a large staphyloma makes axial length measurement and intraocular lens power choice harder.
Assuming refractive surgery removes the risk. The long eye and its retina are unchanged after laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK).
