notes.title: Reading an ocular B-scan
notes.sub: When to scan, and how retina, vitreous and choroid echoes differ

blocks.p: B-scan ultrasonography builds a two-dimensional cross-section of the eye from reflected sound. It usually uses a 10 megahertz (MHz) probe placed on the closed lids with gel. Its main use is to see the back of the eye when you cannot: dense cataract, vitreous haemorrhage, corneal opacity or a small pupil. It also measures and characterises masses, and finds foreign bodies, calcification and optic disc drusen. It shows fluid behind the eye too.

Scan in more than one plane and keep it moving. Kinetic echography (watching echoes move) matters: ask the patient to look away and back, then watch how each echo moves after the eye stops. Reduce the gain (signal amplification) to judge how strongly a membrane reflects.

img.label: vitreous opacities
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with a few faint dots in an otherwise clear vitreous cavity
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: a few low, scattered echoes in an otherwise clear vitreous cavity, consistent with vitreous opacities (floaters).

ul: Vitreous haemorrhage: many fine, mobile echoes that swirl with eye movement and may layer inferiorly.
Posterior vitreous detachment (PVD): a thin, smooth, very mobile membrane that loses its signal at low gain. It may or may not stay attached at the disc.
Retinal detachment: a brighter, thicker, less mobile membrane. It stays attached at the optic disc and the ora serrata (front edge of the retina). A total detachment forms a funnel.
Choroidal detachment: thick, smooth, dome-shaped elevations with little after-movement that do not insert at the disc. Large ones can touch centrally (kissing).

img.label: choroidal detachment
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound showing a curved membrane and a thickened posterior eye wall
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: a curved membrane in front of the posterior pole, with diffuse thickening of the posterior eye wall. It was reported as retinal detachment with choroidal detachment.

img.label: silicone oil emulsification
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with many bright dots scattered through the vitreous cavity
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound of a silicone oil-filled eye: many bright dots scattered through the cavity from emulsified oil droplets.

blocks.p: Silicone oil slows sound, so the posterior wall looks further away and poorly defined. Emulsified oil adds many bright specks. Tenon's space lies between Tenon's capsule and the sclera. A thickened posterior sclera with fluid in Tenon's space outlining the optic nerve forms the T-sign of posterior scleritis.

img.label: tenon's capsule edema
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with a dark curved band behind the back wall of the eye
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: an arc of low reflectivity just behind the posterior eye wall, fluid in Tenon's space. With the optic nerve shadow this makes the T-sign.

ul: Scan every eye with a dense vitreous haemorrhage and no fundal view: a detachment or tear changes the urgency.
Repeat the scan when the view stays poor; a new detachment can develop behind blood.
Masses need standardised A-scan (one-dimensional ultrasound) reflectivity and specialist review, not a single B-scan.
Record the probe position, eye and gain so the next scan can be compared like for like.

blocks.pearl: Follow the membrane to where it inserts: retina anchors at the disc, choroid does not.

ul: Pressing on an eye that may be open: use computed tomography (CT) first. Scan only when the globe is intact or repaired.
Reading a dense PVD as retinal detachment at high gain.
Measuring axial length or tumour height through silicone oil without correcting for the slower sound speed.

sources: Byrne SF, Green RL. Ultrasound of the Eye and Orbit. 2nd ed. St Louis: Mosby; 2002.
McCluskey PJ, Watson PG, Lightman S, et al. Posterior scleritis: clinical features, systemic associations, and outcome in a large series of patients. Ophthalmology 1999;106(12):2380-2386.
Fielding JA. The assessment of ocular injury by ultrasound. Clin Radiol 2004;59(4):301-312.

notes.title: Swollen disc or mimic: papilloedema (optic disc swelling from raised brain pressure) and pseudopapilloedema
notes.sub: Frisen grading, same-day work-up, and the common look-alikes

blocks.p: **Papilloedema** means optic disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure. The optic disc is where the optic nerve leaves the eye. Each optic nerve carries both the nasal and the temporal fibres of its own eye. Papilloedema is usually bilateral, though it can be asymmetric. Disc swelling from other causes, such as optic neuritis or ischaemic optic neuropathy, is called optic disc oedema. It is usually one-sided with early visual loss. Pseudopapilloedema is a disc that looks swollen but is not.

ul: Symptoms of raised intracranial pressure: headache worse lying down or on waking, nausea and pulsatile tinnitus. Also transient visual obscurations (brief greying of vision) and double vision. The double vision comes from a sixth (abducens) cranial nerve palsy. This weakens the lateral rectus, which turns the eye outward.

Early papilloedema spares acuity and colour vision; the blind spot (the field area of the optic disc) enlarges. Loss of acuity or field is a late and serious sign. By then optic nerve damage can cause permanent loss of vision in that eye.

Disc signs: blurred and elevated margins, and vessels obscured as they cross the margin. Also dilated disc capillaries, peripapillary haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, venous engorgement and circumferential retinal folds.
Spontaneous venous pulsation argues against raised pressure, but its absence is common in normal people.

img.label: medullated nerve fibers
img.alt: Fundus photo with white feathery patches radiating from the disc on all sides
img.caption: Colour fundus photograph: white, feathery, striated patches radiate from the disc on all sides. They follow the nerve fibre layer and veil the vessels. These are myelinated (medullated) nerve fibres, a congenital and benign mimic of disc swelling.

blocks.p: Common mimics: optic disc drusen (deposits buried in the disc), myelinated nerve fibres, tilted discs and small crowded discs in hypermetropes. Drusen have lumpy margins and no vessel obscuration. They are visible on enhanced-depth optical coherence tomography (OCT), autofluorescence or ultrasound.

The Frisen scale grades papilloedema from 0 (normal) to 5 (severe). Grading uses the margin, the halo of swollen nerve fibres and obscuration of major vessels at and on the disc. It is useful for follow-up, not for deciding whether swelling is real.

ul: Same day: measure blood pressure to exclude malignant hypertension. Then arrange urgent neuroimaging, ideally magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with magnetic resonance venography. This excludes a mass and venous sinus thrombosis.
If imaging shows no mass, lumbar puncture with opening pressure and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) is diagnosed on the Friedman criteria. These are papilloedema and a normal neurological examination apart from cranial nerve palsies (usually the sixth, abducens). They also need normal imaging and CSF composition, and a raised opening pressure.

IIH care follows the 2018 United Kingdom (UK) consensus. It includes weight management and acetazolamide in selected patients. Urgent surgical or neurosurgical treatment is needed when vision is threatened. Examples are optic nerve sheath fenestration and cerebrospinal fluid shunting.

blocks.pearl: If you cannot decide whether a disc is swollen, you cannot send the patient home: get an urgent ophthalmology or neuro-ophthalmology opinion the same day.

ul: Diagnosing drusen or myelination without imaging and missing true papilloedema.
Accepting a normal computed tomography (CT) scan as the end of the work-up: venous sinus thrombosis needs venography.
Relying on good acuity as reassurance: fields and OCT show damage earlier.
Forgetting old photographs: a disc unchanged for years is not acute papilloedema.

sources: Frisen L. Swelling of the optic nerve head: a staging scheme. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1982;45(1):13-18.
Friedman DI, Liu GT, Digre KB. Revised diagnostic criteria for the pseudotumor cerebri syndrome in adults and children. Neurology 2013;81(13):1159-1165.
Mollan SP, Davies B, Silver NC, et al. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: consensus guidelines on management. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2018;89(10):1088-1100.

Malmqvist L, Bursztyn L, Costello F, et al. The Optic Disc Drusen Studies Consortium recommendations for diagnosis of optic disc drusen using optical coherence tomography. J Neuroophthalmol 2018;38(3):299-307.

notes.title: Uveitis: Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature (SUN) classification and anterior uveitis
notes.sub: Where the inflammation is, how to grade it, first treatment

blocks.p: Uveitis is intraocular inflammation. SUN describes it by where the inflammation is primarily centred. It does not name every structure the inflammation touches:

ul: **Anterior**: anterior chamber (iritis, iridocyclitis).
**Intermediate**: vitreous (includes pars planitis, with snowballs or snowbanking and no systemic cause).
**Posterior**: retina or choroid (retinitis, choroiditis, retinal vasculitis).
**Panuveitis**: anterior chamber, vitreous and retina or choroid together.

blocks.p: SUN also defines the time course. Onset is sudden or insidious. Duration is limited (3 months or less) or persistent (more than 3 months). The course is acute, recurrent or chronic. Recurrent means episodes separated by at least 3 months of inactivity off treatment. Chronic means relapse within 3 months of stopping treatment.

img.label: anterior uveitis
img.alt: Slit-lamp photo of an irregular pupil tethered by iris adhesions to the lens
img.caption: Slit-lamp photograph: posterior synechiae tether the iris to the lens, giving an irregular, notched pupil, with increased density of the lens.

ul: Symptoms: pain, photophobia, redness, blurred vision.

Signs: circumcorneal (ciliary) injection and keratic precipitates (inflammatory cell deposits on the back of the cornea). These are fine, or large mutton-fat in granulomatous disease. Also cells and flare, and fibrin or hypopyon (layer of pus in the front chamber). Look for posterior synechiae (iris stuck to the lens) and iris nodules.
Check intraocular pressure (IOP): it may be low from shutdown of the ciliary body (which makes aqueous). It may be high from inflammation or steroids.
Always look at the vitreous and dilated fundus: anterior signs can be the front of a panuveitis.

img.label: intermediate uveitis
img.alt: Series of fluorescein angiogram frames with leakage from peripheral retinal capillaries
img.caption: Fluorescein angiogram frames: dilated peripheral retinal capillaries leak dye, the angiographic appearance in this eye with intermediate uveitis.

blocks.p: SUN grades anterior chamber cells in a 1 millimetre (mm) by 1 mm slit beam. Grades are 0 (under 1 cell), 0.5+ (1 to 5) and 1+ (6 to 15). Higher grades are 2+ (16 to 25), 3+ (26 to 50) and 4+ (over 50). Flare runs from 0 to 4+ (intense, with fibrin). Improvement is a two-step fall in grade or a fall to zero.

ul: Exclude infection first where suspected (herpes, syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis): steroids alone can make it worse.

Acute anterior uveitis: frequent topical corticosteroid (such as prednisolone acetate) tapered by response. Add a cycloplegic (such as cyclopentolate or atropine) to relieve pain and break or prevent synechiae.

Investigate by pattern, not with a blanket panel. A first unilateral non-granulomatous episode needs little. Recurrent, bilateral, granulomatous or posterior disease needs targeted tests. These include syphilis serology, human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27), chest imaging and tuberculosis testing.

Sight-threatening, chronic or bilateral posterior disease: periocular, intravitreal or systemic steroid. Also steroid-sparing immunosuppression (such as methotrexate or mycophenolate) or biologics (such as adalimumab), with a uveitis specialist.

blocks.pearl: HLA-B27 anterior uveitis is typically sudden, one eye at a time, recurrent and often with fibrin. It is linked to back pain, psoriasis or bowel disease: ask.

ul: Starting topical steroid for a red eye without a slit-lamp view that excludes herpetic keratitis.
Missing cystoid macular oedema (fluid cysts in the central retina), the commonest cause of lasting visual loss in uveitis.
Forgetting that the SUN 2021 classification criteria define specific diseases such as HLA-B27 or sarcoid uveitis. The 2005 descriptors do not.

sources: Jabs DA, Nussenblatt RB, Rosenbaum JT; Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature (SUN) Working Group. Standardization of uveitis nomenclature for reporting clinical data. Results of the First International Workshop. Am J Ophthalmol 2005;140(3):509-516.
Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature (SUN) Working Group. Development of classification criteria for the uveitides. Am J Ophthalmol 2021;228:96-105.
Jaffe GJ, Dick AD, Brezin AP, et al. Adalimumab in patients with active noninfectious uveitis. N Engl J Med 2016;375(10):932-943.

notes.title: Coats disease and familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR)
notes.sub: Exudative look-alikes of retinopathy of prematurity and retinoblastoma

blocks.p: **Coats disease** is an idiopathic retinal telangiectasia: abnormal, leaky retinal vessels flood the retina with lipid-rich exudate. These eventually cause an exudative retinal detachment. It is almost always one-sided and mostly affects boys, often in the first decade.

**Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR)** is an inherited failure of the peripheral retina to vascularise. It is most often autosomal dominant. Genes include frizzled-4 (FZD4), low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 5 (LRP5) and tetraspanin-12 (TSPAN12). It is usually bilateral, often asymmetric, and looks like retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) in a child born at term.

img.label: coats disease
img.alt: Widefield retinal image with extensive yellow exudate around the posterior pole
img.caption: Widefield scanning laser ophthalmoscope image: extensive yellow exudation spreads around the posterior pole. Abnormal telangiectatic vessels lie in the mid-periphery, in Coats disease.

img.label: coats disease
img.alt: Fundus photo with yellow exudate, pigment clumps and elevated retina
img.caption: Colour fundus photograph: massive yellow subretinal exudate with pigment clumping and raised, fluid-filled retina in Coats disease.

ul: Coats: dilated, beaded, light-bulb aneurysms, often temporal and peripheral. Yellow exudate collects at the macula. There may be a yellow reflex (xanthocoria), strabismus (squint) or poor vision.

FEVR: avascular peripheral retina, most often temporal, with straightened vessels ending abruptly. Severe eyes show dragged macula, falciform (sickle-shaped) retinal folds, exudation, neovascularisation and tractional detachment.
Fluorescein angiography shows the telangiectasia and leakage in Coats and the sharp vascular-avascular border in FEVR.
Ultrasound in Coats shows subretinal fluid and exudate without the calcified mass of retinoblastoma. This is a key point when the view is poor.

img.label: familial exudative vitreoretinopathy
img.alt: Series of fluorescein angiogram frames with abrupt peripheral vessel endings and leakage
img.caption: Fluorescein angiogram frames: rigid temporal vessels end abruptly with peripheral non-perfusion. Leaking clusters of small vessels and old laser scars are seen, in FEVR.

blocks.p: Shields staging of Coats disease: 1 telangiectasia only; 2 telangiectasia with exudation (2A away from, 2B involving the fovea); 3 exudative detachment (3A subtotal, 3B total); 4 total detachment with glaucoma; 5 advanced end-stage disease. Visual outcome is best when treatment starts before exudate reaches the fovea. Stage predicts the chance of keeping a useful, comfortable eye.

ul: Any child with leukocoria (white pupil) or xanthocoria is referred urgently to exclude retinoblastoma first.

Coats: close the leaking vessels with laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy, repeated as needed. Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) or steroid injections are sometimes used as adjuncts. Drainage or vitrectomy is used for detachment.
FEVR: laser to the avascular retina when there is leakage or neovascularisation; vitreoretinal surgery for detachment. Examine both eyes of relatives, who are often asymptomatic.
Treat amblyopia (weak vision from disuse in childhood) and follow up long term: both can reactivate.

blocks.pearl: A term-born child with an ROP-like retina has FEVR until proven otherwise: look at the parents' peripheral retina.

ul: Calling a white or yellow reflex Coats disease without excluding retinoblastoma.
Examining only the symptomatic eye in FEVR.
Stopping review after one treatment: new telangiectasia and exudation appear over years.
Missing a Coats-like exudative response in a child or adult with another retinal disease, such as retinitis pigmentosa.

sources: Shields JA, Shields CL, Honavar SG, Demirci H, Cater J. Classification and management of Coats disease: the 2000 Proctor Lecture. Am J Ophthalmol 2001;131(5):572-583.
Gilmour DF. Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy and related retinopathies. Eye 2015;29(1):1-14.
Shields JA, Shields CL. Differentiation of Coats' disease and retinoblastoma. J Pediatr Ophthalmol Strabismus 2001;38(5):262-266.

notes.title: Leukocoria (white pupil) and retinoblastoma
notes.sub: Red reflex, the retinoblastoma 1 gene, no computed tomography, never biopsy

blocks.p: Retinoblastoma is the commonest primary eye cancer of childhood. It is usually found before age 5, and earlier in bilateral disease. It is curable when caught inside the eye, and fatal when it spreads. That is why presentation delay decides outcome worldwide.

It follows loss of both copies of the **RB1** (retinoblastoma 1) tumour suppressor gene. In heritable retinoblastoma one mutation is in every cell. All bilateral cases and a minority of unilateral cases are heritable. In heritable disease the child's own children are at high risk. Non-heritable disease is unilateral and unifocal. Offer genetic testing to every family.

ul: Leukocoria, a white pupil reflex, is the commonest sign. Parents often notice it in flash photographs.
Strabismus (squint) is the second commonest: every new strabismus needs a dilated fundus examination.
Late signs: red painful eye, glaucoma, pseudo-hypopyon (tumour cells layered in the front chamber), orbital inflammation, proptosis (forward bulging of the eye).
Red reflex testing at newborn and infant checks is the screening test. An absent, white or unequal reflex needs referral.

img.label: retinoblastoma
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with a rounded mass arising from the back wall containing bright echoes
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: a well-defined, mushroom-shaped mass rises from the eye wall with bright internal echoes. In a child, bright foci like these suggest calcification. They strongly support retinoblastoma.

blocks.p: Examination under anaesthesia by a retinoblastoma team confirms the diagnosis. Ultrasound shows calcification. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the orbits and brain assesses the optic nerve, extraocular spread and the pineal gland. The optic nerve is a route of spread to the brain. The pineal gland can carry a linked midline tumour (trilateral retinoblastoma). Avoid computed tomography (CT) where possible, because radiation raises second-cancer risk in heritable disease.

The International Intraocular Retinoblastoma Classification groups eyes A to E and predicts eye salvage. Group A is small tumours away from fovea and disc. Group E is extensive disease, with the eye not salvageable. The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition tumour, node, metastasis, heritability (TNMH) system adds staging for spread. It also records heritable trait (H).

ul: Urgent referral to a retinoblastoma centre. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guideline 12 (NG12) advises urgent referral for an absent red reflex.
Priorities in order: life, the eye, then vision.

Options: intravenous chemotherapy (carboplatin, etoposide and vincristine), or intra-arterial or intravitreal chemotherapy (melphalan). Others are laser or cryotherapy, plaque brachytherapy, and enucleation for advanced eyes. External beam radiotherapy is avoided where possible.
Offer screening to siblings and future children of heritable cases. Follow up lifelong for second cancers such as osteosarcoma, soft tissue sarcomas and melanoma.

blocks.pearl: A parent who says the pupil looks white in photos is right until proven otherwise: refer urgently, do not reassure.

ul: Needle biopsy or vitrectomy of an eye that may contain retinoblastoma: it can seed tumour outside the eye.
Treating strabismus in a child without a dilated fundus view.
Forgetting the differentials of leukocoria: Coats disease, persistent fetal vasculature, retinopathy of prematurity, toxocariasis, congenital cataract, coloboma.

sources: Murphree AL. Intraocular retinoblastoma: the case for a new group classification. Ophthalmol Clin North Am 2005;18(1):41-53.
Dimaras H, Corson TW, Cobrinik D, et al. Retinoblastoma. Nat Rev Dis Primers 2015;1:15021.
Mallipatna AC, Gallie BL, Chevez-Barrios P, et al. Retinoblastoma. In: Amin MB, et al., eds. AJCC Cancer Staging Manual. 8th ed. New York: Springer; 2017:819-831.
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (NG12). London: NICE; 2015.

notes.title: Ocular trauma: first steps
notes.sub: Chemicals first, protect an open globe, image before you scan

blocks.p: Eye injuries range from a harmless subconjunctival haemorrhage to a globe rupture. The first minutes decide which eyes can be saved, so a clear sequence matters more than detailed examination. The Birmingham Eye Trauma Terminology (BETT) gives a shared language. A **closed globe** injury (contusion or lamellar laceration) has no full-thickness wound. An **open globe** injury is either a rupture from blunt force or a laceration from a sharp object. A laceration may be penetrating (entry wound only), perforating (entry and exit) or carry an intraocular foreign body.

ul: Chemical injury: treat before examining. Irrigate at once with saline or clean water and evert the lids. Sweep the fornices and continue until the pH is neutral on repeated checks. Alkali burns are the most dangerous.

Open globe: a full-thickness wound, a peaked pupil, a shallow or deep anterior chamber. Also uveal prolapse and a positive Seidel test (fluorescein shows aqueous leaking from the wound). Other signs are a soft eye and extensive haemorrhagic chemosis (bloody conjunctival swelling).
High-velocity injury such as hammering metal on metal: assume an intraocular foreign body.
Record visual acuity and pupil reactions (relative afferent pupillary defect, RAPD) early. They carry prognosis, as captured in the Ocular Trauma Score.

img.label: subconjunctival hemorrhage
img.alt: Photo of a flat bright-red patch on the white of the eye next to the cornea
img.caption: Slit-lamp photograph: a flat, bright-red, well-demarcated subconjunctival haemorrhage on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva, with a clear cornea. It is harmless on its own. After injury it is harmless only when vision, pupil and anterior chamber are normal and its back edge is visible.

img.label: foreign body in the vitreous cavity
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with a bright spot and a shadow behind it inside the eye
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: a foreign body in the vitreous. A very bright echo in front of the posterior eye wall casts an acoustic shadow, with dense vitreous echoes. Scan gently, and only once an open globe has been excluded or repaired. Computed tomography (CT) comes first.

ul: Suspected open globe: rigid shield without pressure, no drops or ointment, nil by mouth, analgesia and antiemetic. Check tetanus status, give systemic antibiotics per local protocol and refer urgently for primary repair.
Imaging: computed tomography (CT) of the orbits to find a foreign body. No magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) while a metallic foreign body is possible.

Hyphaema (blood in the front chamber): rest with head raised, shield, topical steroid and cycloplegic. Check intraocular pressure (IOP) daily, and sickle cell status in at-risk patients. Watch for a rebleed.

Orbital floor fracture: check eye movements and infraorbital sensation (supplied by the infraorbital nerve). A child with a trapped inferior rectus, nausea and a slow pulse needs urgent surgery, even with a white eye. The nausea and slow pulse are the oculocardiac reflex.

Retrobulbar haemorrhage with a tense orbit, falling vision and RAPD: lateral canthotomy and cantholysis immediately, before imaging. The orbital pressure compresses the optic nerve and can cause permanent loss of vision in that eye.

blocks.pearl: In a chemical injury, water comes before visual acuity: irrigate first, assess second.

ul: Pressing on the eye to open the lids or scan it before an open globe is excluded.
Missing a small scleral rupture hidden under a large haemorrhagic chemosis.
Discharging a hammering injury without imaging for an intraocular foreign body.

sources: Kuhn F, Morris R, Witherspoon CD, Heimann K, Jeffers JB, Treister G. A standardized classification of ocular trauma. Ophthalmology 1996;103(2):240-243.
Kuhn F, Maisiak R, Mann L, Mester V, Morris R, Witherspoon CD. The Ocular Trauma Score (OTS). Ophthalmol Clin North Am 2002;15(2):163-165.
Dua HS, King AJ, Joseph A. A new classification of ocular surface burns. Br J Ophthalmol 2001;85(11):1379-1383.

notes.title: Reading the optic disc for glaucoma
notes.sub: Disc size first, then the rim, notches, haemorrhages and the nerve fibre layer

blocks.p: Glaucoma is an optic neuropathy (disease of the optic nerve): retinal ganglion cell axons are lost, the neuroretinal rim thins and the cup enlarges. These axons form the optic nerve, which carries both the nasal and the temporal fibres of its own eye. Lost axons do not recover, so the field loss in that eye is permanent. The disc often changes before the patient notices any field loss. So a careful disc examination is the most useful screening skill in glaucoma. Examine both discs stereoscopically at the slit lamp with a 78 dioptre (D) or 90 D lens. Compare the two eyes.
Work through the disc in the same order every time.

ul: **Disc size.** Estimate it first, from the slit beam height against the disc (corrected for the lens used). Large discs have large physiological cups; small discs can hide real damage behind a small cup.

**Neuroretinal rim** (the band of nerve fibres between the cup and the disc edge). A healthy rim is pink and usually follows the inferior, superior, nasal, temporal (ISNT) pattern. It is thickest inferiorly, then superiorly, nasally and temporally. Glaucoma thins the rim first at the inferior and superior poles. So an eye that breaks ISNT deserves a closer look.
**Vertical cup-to-disc ratio (CDR).** Judge the cup by the bend of the small vessels, not by pallor. An asymmetry of more than 0.2 between eyes with similar disc sizes is suspicious.

**Focal signs.** A notch in the rim, and a splinter haemorrhage crossing the rim edge. Also bayoneting (sharp double bend) of vessels as they dip over a thin rim. Baring of the circumlinear vessels (vessels that run along the cup edge) is another sign.

**Around the disc.** Beta-zone peripapillary atrophy (bare sclera and large choroidal vessels visible next to the disc margin). Also wedge-shaped dark defects in the retinal nerve fibre layer (RNFL), best seen with red-free light.

img.label: normal
img.alt: Optic disc with a small central cup and a pink rim all around
img.caption: Healthy disc: a central cup surrounded by a pink neuroretinal rim all the way round. Vessels leave the centre of the disc.

img.label: glaucoma
img.alt: Optic disc with a very large pale cup and a thin rim
img.caption: Glaucomatous disc: the cup occupies almost the whole disc. The rim is reduced to a thin crescent at the margin and the vessels are pushed to one edge.

blocks.p: The Disc Damage Likelihood Scale (DDLS) grades the narrowest rim width relative to disc size. This corrects for the large-disc and small-disc traps of the CDR. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) measures the peripapillary nerve fibre layer and the macular ganglion cell complex. The ganglion cell complex is the inner retinal layers that hold the ganglion cells. OCT adds an objective, repeatable measure. But it is compared with a normative database that may not match your patient.

A suspicious disc is not a diagnosis. It needs intraocular pressure (IOP) with corneal thickness, gonioscopy, standard automated perimetry and OCT. Then decide whether this is glaucoma, a glaucoma suspect or a normal variant. Photograph or image the disc as a baseline, because change over time is the strongest evidence of glaucoma.

blocks.pearl: Size the disc before you judge the cup: a CDR of 0.7 can be normal in a large disc, and 0.4 can be glaucomatous in a small one.

ul: Rim pallor out of proportion to cupping suggests a non-glaucomatous optic neuropathy, such as compression of the optic nerve. That eye needs neuroimaging, not just IOP-lowering drops.
Tilted, myopic discs with wide atrophy are hard to read and give unreliable OCT results.
A disc haemorrhage is easy to miss and fades within weeks; look for it at every visit.
One photograph cannot show progression; compare with earlier images of the same eye.

sources: European Glaucoma Society. Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 5th Edition. Br J Ophthalmol 2021;105(Suppl 1):1-169.
Jonas JB, Gusek GC, Naumann GO. Optic disc, cup and neuroretinal rim size, configuration and correlations in normal eyes. Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 1988;29(7):1151-1158.

Spaeth GL, Henderer J, Liu C, et al. The disc damage likelihood scale: reproducibility of a new method of estimating the amount of optic nerve damage caused by glaucoma. Trans Am Ophthalmol Soc 2002;100:181-185.
Gedde SJ, Bowden EC, Challa P, et al. Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2026;133(4):P1-P103.

notes.title: Primary open-angle glaucoma
notes.sub: Diagnosis needs disc, field and an open angle; treat to a target

blocks.p: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a chronic, progressive optic neuropathy. It has characteristic disc and nerve fibre layer damage, matching visual field loss and an open drainage angle. The drainage angle is where the trabecular meshwork drains aqueous. There is no secondary cause such as pigment dispersion, pseudoexfoliation or steroids. Intraocular pressure (IOP) is often raised but not always: normal-tension glaucoma sits at one end of the same spectrum. It is painless and central vision is kept until late. That is why so many people are diagnosed only when damage is advanced. The field loss it causes is permanent.
Risk factors: raised IOP (the only one we can treat), older age and a family history. Others are African or Caribbean ancestry, myopia and a thin central cornea.

img.label: glaucoma
img.alt: Optic disc with a large cup, a thin rim and vessels bending at the cup edge
img.caption: Glaucomatous disc: a large, deep cup with a thin rim; the vessels bend sharply as they climb out over the cup edge.

img.label: glaucoma
img.alt: Optic disc with an enlarged cup and a vessel kinking over the rim
img.caption: Glaucomatous disc: an enlarged cup with a thinned rim, and a vessel that kinks where it crosses the cup margin (bayoneting).

ul: Disc: enlarged vertical cup, rim notching or thinning, disc haemorrhage, nerve fibre layer defects.
Field: arcuate or nasal step defects that respect the horizontal meridian and match the disc.
Angle: open on gonioscopy (viewing the angle through a mirrored contact lens). Never label glaucoma open-angle without looking at the angle.
IOP: measured with Goldmann applanation tonometry, interpreted with central corneal thickness.

blocks.p: Set a target pressure for each eye. Base it on the pressure at which damage occurred, the stage of disease, the rate of progression and life expectancy. The American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) guideline suggests a reasonable initial goal of 20 to 30% below the untreated pressure. It is adjusted up or down as the course unfolds. Lowering pressure works. In the Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial, each 1 millimetre of mercury (mmHg) of reduction cut progression risk by about 10%. In the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study, treatment roughly halved the 5-year risk of developing glaucoma.

ul: First line: a prostaglandin analogue drop (such as latanoprost), or selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT). In the Laser in Glaucoma and Ocular Hypertension (LiGHT) trial, most eyes given SLT first were drop-free at 3 years. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) now offers SLT first.

Add or switch drops when the target is not met. Options are a beta-blocker (timolol), a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (dorzolamide or brinzolamide) or an alpha agonist (brimonidine). Check for asthma and bradycardia before a beta-blocker.

Surgery is used when the target is not reached or damage is advanced. Options are trabeculectomy with an antimetabolite (mitomycin C or 5-fluorouracil), a tube shunt, or selected minimally invasive procedures.
Monitor with fields and optical coherence tomography (OCT) at intervals set by the stage and rate of change.

blocks.pearl: Before calling it progression, ask whether the patient is using the drops. Poor adherence and poor drop technique are the commonest reasons a target is missed.

ul: Skipping gonioscopy and treating angle closure as open-angle glaucoma.
A thin cornea makes the measured pressure read low; a thick one makes it read high.
Normal-tension glaucoma with atypical features needs neuroimaging. These features are young age, pallor greater than cupping, or a field that respects the vertical meridian.
One field test is not enough; the first is often unreliable because of learning effects.

notes.title: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP): International Classification of ROP, third edition (ICROP3) zones, stages and plus
notes.sub: Where it is, how far it has gone, how sick the vessels look

blocks.p: ROP is a vasoproliferative disease (abnormal new vessel growth) of the incompletely vascularised retina of preterm infants. Retinal vessels normally reach the ora serrata (the front edge of the retina) near term. A baby born early has an avascular periphery. Abnormal growth at the junction between vascular and avascular retina can progress to traction and detachment. ICROP3 (2021) describes each eye by zone, stage, extent in clock hours and plus disease.

ul: **Zone I:** a circle centred on the disc with a radius twice the disc-to-fovea distance.
**Posterior zone II:** new in ICROP3, a band two disc diameters wide just outside zone I. Disease here behaves more like zone I.
**Zone II:** from zone I out to the nasal ora serrata.
**Zone III:** the remaining temporal crescent.
A **notch** is a 1 to 2 clock-hour incursion of disease into a more posterior zone. It is recorded as, for example, zone I secondary to notch.

img.label: s1
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with vascularised retina near the disc and a pale avascular periphery
img.caption: Stage 1 (born at 28 weeks, weighing 1,000 grams): vessels around the disc stop short of a grey avascular periphery, with a thin flat pale line at the border.

img.label: s2
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with a thin white raised ridge on the right
img.caption: Stage 2 (born at 27 weeks, 950 g): the border between vascular and avascular retina has become a white ridge.

img.label: s3
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with a thick ridge and vessels branching into it
img.caption: Stage 3 (born at 26 weeks, 900 g): a thick, ragged ridge with vessels fanning into it.

img.label: s4
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with a white fibrovascular band arching above the disc
img.caption: Stage 4 (born at 28 weeks, 1,100 g): a thick white fibrovascular band arches above the disc. At this stage the retina is partly detached.

ul: **Stage 1:** a thin, flat, white demarcation line.
**Stage 2:** a ridge with height and width; small isolated tufts may sit behind it.
**Stage 3:** extraretinal neovascular proliferation (new vessels growing off the retina) from the ridge into the vitreous.
**Stage 4:** partial retinal detachment, 4A sparing the fovea, 4B involving it.
**Stage 5:** total detachment. 5A has the disc still visible (open funnel). 5B has retrolental tissue hiding the disc. 5C has anterior segment changes as well.

blocks.p: Plus disease is dilation and tortuosity of the vessels within zone I. ICROP3 treats it as a spectrum from normal through pre-plus to plus. It is judged on the posterior vessels rather than by counting quadrants. **Aggressive ROP (A-ROP)** replaces the older term aggressive posterior ROP (AP-ROP). It is rapidly developing, flat neovascularisation with severe plus disease that does not step through the usual stages. It is typically posterior but can occur in larger, more mature babies. ICROP3 also names regression, reactivation and persistent avascular retina, which matter after treatment.

blocks.pearl: Zone and plus decide urgency more than stage does. A subtle zone I eye with plus disease can need treatment sooner than a peripheral stage 3 ridge.

ul: Vessels simply ending in the periphery is immaturity, not ROP, until a line or ridge appears.
Wide-field images tilt easily, which can make the zone look more peripheral than it is.
The flat neovascular network of A-ROP is easy to overlook because there is no obvious ridge.

sources: Chiang MF, Quinn GE, Fielder AR, et al. International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, Third Edition. Ophthalmology 2021;128(10):e51-e68.
International Committee for the Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity. The International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity revisited. Arch Ophthalmol 2005;123(7):991-999.

Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity Cooperative Group. Revised indications for the treatment of retinopathy of prematurity: results of the Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity randomized trial. Arch Ophthalmol 2003;121(12):1684-1694.

notes.title: Treating retinopathy of prematurity (ROP): Type 1, aggressive ROP (A-ROP) and after laser
notes.sub: Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity Type 1, laser or injection

blocks.p: Treatment aims to stop the vasoproliferative drive before traction detaches the retina. Since the Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity (ETROP) trial (2003), the decision rests on the ETROP risk types rather than on the older threshold disease. Treatment is given promptly once an eye qualifies.

ul: **Type 1 ROP, treat:** zone I, any stage, with plus disease; zone I, stage 3, without plus; zone II, stage 2 or 3, with plus disease.
**Type 2 ROP, watch closely:** zone I, stage 1 or 2, without plus; zone II, stage 3, without plus. Treat if it progresses to Type 1.
**A-ROP:** treat urgently; do not wait for the classic stages to appear.

blocks.p: Treat Type 1 disease as soon as practical, generally within 48 to 72 hours of the decision.

img.label: arop
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with dilated tortuous vessels and haemorrhages around the disc
img.caption: A-ROP (born at 28 weeks, 1,500 grams): markedly dilated and tortuous posterior vessels with scattered haemorrhages, and no well-formed ridge.

img.label: laser
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with rows of pale laser scars in the periphery
img.caption: After laser (born at 27 weeks, 950 g): dense pale laser scars cover the peripheral avascular retina, next to the vascularised retina.

ul: **Laser photocoagulation** of the entire avascular retina, near-confluent, through an indirect ophthalmoscope. It is the long-standing standard and its effect is permanent. But it destroys peripheral retina and is linked to more myopia.

**Intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF)** (bevacizumab or ranibizumab) is quicker, easier in very posterior disease and lets vessels keep growing. In the Bevacizumab Eliminates the Angiogenic Threat of ROP (BEAT-ROP) trial (2011), bevacizumab reduced recurrence compared with laser. This was for zone I stage 3 with plus, but not for zone II disease. A 2019 trial tested ranibizumab against laser: Ranibizumab Compared With Laser Therapy for the Treatment of Infants Born Prematurely With Retinopathy of Prematurity (RAINBOW). In RAINBOW, ranibizumab showed a trend towards more treatment success than laser. The trend narrowly missed statistical significance.

After anti-VEGF, disease can reactivate weeks to months later. Long-term systemic safety in preterm infants is still being studied. Follow these babies for longer, until vascularisation is complete or the retina is stable. Consider laser to persistent avascular retina.
Stage 4 and 5 disease needs a vitreoretinal surgeon: lens-sparing vitrectomy or scleral buckling in selected eyes.

blocks.p: Every treated baby needs long-term eye care. Myopia and anisometropia (unequal refraction between the eyes), strabismus, amblyopia and late retinal detachment are all more common. This holds even when the retina looks quiet.

blocks.pearl: An injection buys time, not closure. A baby treated with anti-VEGF needs examinations for months longer than a lasered one. A missed follow-up can cost the eye.

ul: Waiting for stage 3 in a zone I eye with plus disease; plus alone makes zone I disease Type 1.
Skip areas left untreated at the edge of the laser can let disease progress; re-examine within a week or two.
Discharging an injected baby from ROP follow-up once the neonatal unit closes the file.

sources: Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity Cooperative Group. Revised indications for the treatment of retinopathy of prematurity: results of the Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity randomized trial. Arch Ophthalmol 2003;121(12):1684-1694.
Mintz-Hittner HA, Kennedy KA, Chuang AZ; BEAT-ROP Cooperative Group. Efficacy of intravitreal bevacizumab for stage 3+ retinopathy of prematurity. N Engl J Med 2011;364(7):603-615.

Chiang MF, Quinn GE, Fielder AR, et al. International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, Third Edition. Ophthalmology 2021;128(10):e51-e68.
Fierson WM; American Academy of Pediatrics Section on Ophthalmology, et al. Screening examination of premature infants for retinopathy of prematurity. Pediatrics 2018;142(6):e20183061.

notes.title: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) screening: who, when and how
notes.sub: Criteria by country, the first exam, intervals and when to stop

blocks.p: Blinding ROP is largely preventable: treatment works if the disease is found in time. Screening is a timed series of dilated retinal examinations of at-risk preterm babies. It continues until the retina has vascularised or the disease has regressed. Most eyes screened never need treatment. But a missed or late examination is the commonest route to a blind child.

ul: **United Kingdom (UK, 2022 guideline):** all babies born before 31 weeks gestation or weighing less than 1,501 grams.

**United States of America (USA), American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) 2018:** birth weight 1,500 g or less, or gestation 30 weeks or less. Also selected larger or more mature babies with an unstable clinical course.

**India and other middle-income settings:** national criteria are wider. Larger and more mature babies develop severe ROP where oxygen delivery and monitoring are less controlled. Follow your national guideline.

blocks.p: Risk rises with lower gestation and birth weight. It also rises with unmonitored or fluctuating oxygen, sepsis, poor postnatal weight gain and a stormy neonatal course.

The AAP schedule sets the timing of the first examination. It is at 31 weeks postmenstrual age (PMA) or 4 weeks after birth, whichever is later. This means the most premature babies are not examined before disease can appear. Follow-up intervals then depend on the findings. Examine weekly or more often for zone I, posterior zone II or any plus disease. Examine every 2 to 3 weeks for mild, peripheral findings or immature retina in zone III.

img.label: normal
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with a normal disc and vessels
img.caption: No ROP in a baby born at 30 weeks weighing 1,200 g: the disc and vessels look normal, with no dilated or tortuous vessels and no line or ridge in this view.

blocks.p: At each visit record the zone of vascularisation or disease, and the stage and its extent in clock hours. Also record the presence of pre-plus or plus disease. Use the International Classification of ROP, third edition (ICROP3) terms, so the next examiner can compare.

ul: Dilate with drops at low concentration suitable for neonates, such as cyclopentolate 0.5% with phenylephrine 2.5%. Use topical anaesthetic (such as proxymetacaine), a neonatal speculum and scleral indentation, with binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy.
Wide-field digital imaging, read by an ophthalmologist on site or remotely, is an accepted alternative where examiners are scarce.
The examination is stressful: use comfort measures, and have the neonatal team watch for apnoea and bradycardia.

blocks.p: Stop when the retina is vascularised into zone III without previous zone I or II disease. Also stop when vascularisation reaches the ora serrata (the front edge of the retina). Or stop when ROP has clearly regressed with no abnormal tissue left that could reactivate. Babies treated with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) need longer follow-up.

blocks.pearl: The screening schedule is the treatment. Most children blinded by ROP had a treatable disease that was examined too late or not at all.

ul: Losing babies at transfer or discharge; book the next examination before the baby leaves.
Using another country's criteria and missing larger at-risk babies.
Recording an immature retina as normal and stopping too early.

sources: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, Royal College of Ophthalmologists, British Association of Perinatal Medicine. UK Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity. 2022.
Fierson WM; American Academy of Pediatrics Section on Ophthalmology, et al. Screening examination of premature infants for retinopathy of prematurity. Pediatrics 2018;142(6):e20183061.
Chiang MF, Quinn GE, Fielder AR, et al. International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, Third Edition. Ophthalmology 2021;128(10):e51-e68.

notes.title: Microbial keratitis: bacterial, fungal, acanthamoeba, herpetic
notes.sub: Clues to the organism, scrape first, and when steroids harm

blocks.p: Microbial keratitis is infection of the cornea, usually through a break in the epithelium. It is an emergency: a central ulcer can scar, thin or perforate within days. Contact lens wear is the main risk factor in high-income countries. Trauma, often with vegetable matter, dominates in agricultural regions, including much of India.

img.label: severe keratitis with a corneal ulcer
img.alt: Red, swollen eye with a hazy cornea and a white ulcer in the lower cornea
img.caption: Slit lamp: intense conjunctival redness and swelling, a hazy, oedematous cornea and a white ulcerated infiltrate in the lower cornea.

ul: **Bacterial:** rapid onset, pain, discharge and an epithelial defect over a dense white stromal infiltrate. Often there is a hypopyon (layer of pus in the front chamber). Common organisms are Staphylococcus, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Pseudomonas. Pseudomonas is the classic organism in contact lens wearers.
**Fungal:** slower, often after plant trauma; usually Fusarium or Aspergillus. Look for a dry, greyish infiltrate with feathery margins, satellite lesions and sometimes an endothelial plaque.
**Acanthamoeba:** contact lens wear with water exposure; pain out of proportion to the signs, early patchy epitheliopathy, radial perineural infiltrates and later a ring infiltrate.
**Herpes simplex epithelial:** a branching dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs that stains with fluorescein. Corneal sensation (from the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve) is reduced.

blocks.p: Take a corneal scrape for Gram and fungal stains and cultures before starting intensive treatment, without delaying it; send the contact lenses and case too. Then treat by the likely organism under your local protocol.

ul: Bacterial: intensive topical broad-spectrum antibiotic. Use a fluoroquinolone (such as moxifloxacin), or fortified antibiotics (such as cefazolin with tobramycin) for severe ulcers. Give it day and night at first, tapered by response. The Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial (SCUT, 2012) added a topical steroid after 48 hours of antibiotic. This gave no overall benefit in vision.
Fungal: topical natamycin for filamentous fungi. The first Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trial (MUTT, 2013), known as MUTT I, found natamycin better than voriconazole, mainly for Fusarium. No steroids.
Acanthamoeba: a topical biguanide, polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) or chlorhexidine, often with a diamidine (propamidine). Treatment runs for months under a cornea specialist.
Herpetic epithelial disease: topical antiviral (ganciclovir gel or aciclovir ointment) or oral aciclovir. Steroids are for stromal disease only, under antiviral cover.

blocks.p: Add a cycloplegic for pain, stop contact lens wear, and review daily at first. Increasing thinning, a descemetocele (Descemet membrane bulging where the stroma is lost) or perforation needs a cornea surgeon: glue, a patch graft or a therapeutic keratoplasty.

blocks.pearl: A contact lens wearer with a painful red eye has keratitis until the slit lamp shows otherwise. They need to be seen that day.

ul: Steroid-antibiotic combination drops in an undiagnosed ulcer can let fungal or herpetic infection spread.
Acanthamoeba pseudodendrites are often treated as herpes for weeks; think of it in any lens wearer who is not improving.
Scraping after days of antibiotic lowers culture yield; if the ulcer is not responding, re-scrape or consider a biopsy.

sources: Rhee MK, Ahmad S, Amescua G, et al. Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2024;131(4):P87-P133.
Srinivasan M, Mascarenhas J, Rajaraman R, et al. Corticosteroids for bacterial keratitis: the Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial (SCUT). Arch Ophthalmol 2012;130(2):143-150.
Prajna NV, Krishnan T, Mascarenhas J, et al. The Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trial: a randomized trial comparing natamycin vs voriconazole. JAMA Ophthalmol 2013;131(4):422-429.
Wilhelmus KR, Gee L, Hauck WW, et al. Herpetic Eye Disease Study: a controlled trial of topical corticosteroids for herpes simplex stromal keratitis. Ophthalmology 1994;101(12):1883-1895.

notes.title: Red eye: conjunctivitis, subconjunctival haemorrhage and red flags
notes.sub: The common benign causes, and when a red eye needs same-day care

blocks.p: Most red eyes are benign: conjunctivitis and subconjunctival haemorrhage account for many of them. The skill is to recognise these quickly and pick out the few that threaten sight. These include keratitis, anterior uveitis, acute angle closure, scleritis and trauma.

img.label: conjunctivitis
img.alt: Red, swollen conjunctiva around the lower eyelid with a clear cornea
img.caption: Slit lamp: the conjunctiva is red and swollen, most of all along the lower lid, with some discharge; the cornea is clear.

ul: **Viral (usually adenovirus):** watery discharge, follicles, often a tender preauricular node; the second eye is often affected days later. Very contagious.
**Bacterial:** mucopurulent discharge and lids stuck together on waking; usually self-limiting.
**Allergic:** itching above all, both eyes, papillae and chemosis (conjunctival swelling), often with hay fever or atopy.
**Hyperacute:** copious pus within hours suggests gonococcus (Neisseria gonorrhoeae), which can perforate the cornea. It needs same-day care and systemic treatment.
**Neonatal conjunctivitis** in the first month of life is urgent: swab for gonococcus and chlamydia (Chlamydia trachomatis).

img.label: subconjunctival hemorrhage
img.alt: White eye with a flat bright red patch of blood under the conjunctiva
img.caption: Slit lamp: a flat, sharply bordered patch of bright red blood under the conjunctiva on one side of the cornea; the rest of the eye looks quiet.

blocks.p: A **subconjunctival haemorrhage** is painless, flat and bright red, and vision is normal. It follows coughing, straining or minor rubbing, or occurs with no cause. It fades over one to three weeks without treatment.

ul: Viral: hygiene, cool compresses and lubricants; avoid sharing towels; no routine antibiotics.
Bacterial: a topical antibiotic (such as chloramphenicol) can shorten the illness; delayed or no treatment is reasonable in mild cases.
Allergic: avoid triggers, topical antihistamine (such as olopatadine) or mast cell stabiliser (such as sodium cromoglicate).
Subconjunctival haemorrhage: reassure; check blood pressure, and ask about anticoagulants and bleeding if it recurs or is extensive.
After trauma, a haemorrhage whose back edge you cannot see may hide an open globe or orbital fracture: examine fully.

blocks.h: Red flags: refer the same day

ul: Reduced vision, moderate or severe pain, or photophobia.
Redness concentrated around the cornea (ciliary flush), a corneal opacity or staining.
An abnormal pupil, a raised intraocular pressure, or a hazy cornea with headache and vomiting.
Contact lens wear, recent eye surgery, chemical injury, or a newborn.
Severe, boring pain with a deep violet redness that does not blanch, which suggests scleritis.

blocks.pearl: Conjunctivitis rarely reduces vision or causes real pain. If either is present, look for keratitis, iritis or angle closure before calling it conjunctivitis.

ul: Repeated steroid drops for a red eye without a slit lamp examination.
Missing herpes simplex in a unilateral red eye with watery discharge and lid vesicles.
Treating chronic unilateral follicular conjunctivitis as viral without considering chlamydia.

sources: Cheung AY, Choi DS, Ahmad S, et al. Conjunctivitis Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2024;131(4):P134-P204.
Azari AA, Barney NP. Conjunctivitis: a systematic review of diagnosis and treatment. JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729.

notes.title: Pterygium and other ocular surface growths
notes.sub: Pterygium, suspicious lesions, limbal dermoid and conjunctivalisation

blocks.p: A growth at the limbus (the corneal edge) is usually benign. But the same position is shared by ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN). This note covers the common pterygium, the congenital limbal dermoid, and conjunctivalisation of the cornea after limbal stem cell failure.

img.label: pterygium
img.alt: Grey wedge of tissue growing from the conjunctiva onto the edge of the cornea
img.caption: Slit lamp: a greyish, vascularised wedge of conjunctiva growing across the limbus onto the cornea, within the open lid fissure.

blocks.p: A pterygium is a wedge of fibrovascular conjunctiva growing onto the cornea within the palpebral fissure. It usually grows from the nasal side. Ultraviolet light, heat and dust are the main risks. It can cause irritation, redness, cosmetic concern and astigmatism. It threatens vision when it approaches the visual axis. A **pinguecula** is a yellowish nodule of the bulbar conjunctiva that does not cross the limbus.

ul: Suspect OSSN when a lesion is gelatinous, white and plaque-like, or papillomatous. Also suspect it with large feeder vessels, a site outside the fissure, quick growth or recurrence. The same applies with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection or immunosuppression. Excise with histology.
Surgery for pterygium: excision with a conjunctival autograft, fixed with fibrin glue or sutures. This recurs less often than leaving bare sclera. Mitomycin C is an adjunct in some hands.
Otherwise: lubricants and ultraviolet protection.

img.label: limbal dermoid
img.alt: Smooth dome-shaped yellow-white lump straddling the lower edge of the cornea
img.caption: Slit lamp: a smooth, dome-shaped, yellow-white lump straddling the limbus at the lower edge of the cornea.

blocks.p: A congenital choristoma (normal tissue in an abnormal place), usually at the inferotemporal limbus, sometimes with fine hairs. Look for preauricular tags and facial asymmetry. It can be part of the oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum (Goldenhar syndrome). The main threat is astigmatism and amblyopia (weak vision from disuse in childhood). So refraction and amblyopia treatment come first. Excision is for vision or appearance, knowing the lesion can extend deep into the stroma.

img.label: corneal conjunctivalization
img.alt: Cornea covered by opaque tissue with blood vessels growing across it
img.caption: Slit lamp: conjunctival tissue and new vessels have grown across and cover the cornea.

blocks.p: Limbal stem cells sit at the corneal edge and renew the corneal epithelium. When they fail, conjunctival epithelium and vessels grow over the cornea. Causes include chemical and thermal burns, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and mucous membrane pemphigoid. Others are aniridia, contact lens overuse and repeated surgery. Signs include loss of the limbal palisades of Vogt, late whorled fluorescein staining, vascularisation and recurrent epithelial defects. A corneal graft alone fails: the limbus must be restored first. One example is simple limbal epithelial transplantation (SLET) from the healthy eye in unilateral disease.

blocks.pearl: Any limbal lesion with an atypical site, a white plaque or quick growth is OSSN until histology says otherwise.

ul: Excising a pterygium with bare sclera and getting a faster, more aggressive recurrence.
Treating a dermoid as cosmetic and missing amblyopia.
Offering a penetrating graft to an eye with total limbal stem cell deficiency.

sources: Clearfield E, Muthappan V, Wang X, Kuo IC. Conjunctival autograft for pterygium. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;2:CD011349.

Sangwan VS, Basu S, MacNeil S, Balasubramanian D. Simple limbal epithelial transplantation (SLET): a novel surgical technique for the treatment of unilateral limbal stem cell deficiency. Br J Ophthalmol 2012;96(7):931-934.

notes.title: Cataract and cataract surgery
notes.sub: Types, when to operate, the operation and what can go wrong

blocks.p: A cataract is any opacity of the crystalline lens. Age-related cataract is the leading cause of blindness worldwide and one of the most successfully treated: surgery restores sight in most eyes.

img.label: cataract
img.alt: Eye with a grey-white opacity filling the lens behind the pupil
img.caption: Slit lamp: a grey-white opacity fills the lens behind the pupil.

ul: **Nuclear:** yellow-brown central hardening; distance blur and a myopic shift, sometimes briefly improving reading.
**Cortical:** spoke-like opacities from the periphery; glare from headlights.

**Posterior subcapsular:** a plaque at the back of the lens. It occurs in younger patients, after steroids, and in diabetes, uveitis or radiation. Symptoms are out of proportion to its size, especially in bright light and for reading.
**Congenital and paediatric:** an emergency for amblyopia (weak vision from disuse in childhood). Check the red reflex in every newborn.

blocks.p: Operate on the patient's visual needs, not on the grade of the lens. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) advises against restricting surgery by visual acuity alone. Measure acuity, and examine the dilated lens and the fundus. Look for co-existing disease that limits the result, such as macular degeneration or diabetic macular oedema. Optical biometry (axial length and keratometry) sets the intraocular lens (IOL) power. Agree a refractive target with the patient.

Phacoemulsification is the standard. It uses a small incision and a foldable IOL in the capsular bag, under topical or local anaesthesia. Manual small-incision cataract surgery (MSICS) gives excellent results at low cost. It is widely used in high-volume settings. Intracameral antibiotic at the end of surgery lowers the risk of endophthalmitis (infection inside the eye). This was first shown with cefuroxime in the European Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgeons (ESCRS) study.

ul: During surgery: posterior capsule rupture with vitreous loss, and dropped lens fragments.

After surgery: endophthalmitis (rare but sight-threatening, presenting with pain and falling vision within days). Others are cystoid macular oedema, raised intraocular pressure, retinal detachment (more in high myopia) and refractive surprise.
Posterior capsule opacification months to years later is common. It is cleared with a neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet (Nd:YAG) laser capsulotomy.

img.label: dislocated intraocular lens
img.alt: Dilated pupil with the edge of an intraocular lens crossing it and a torn capsule
img.caption: Slit lamp: the edge of an IOL crosses the pupil. A tear in the posterior capsule suggests the lens has slipped out of the bag.

img.label: intraocular lens (iol) dislocation
img.alt: Fundus with an intraocular lens lying on the lower retina
img.caption: Fundus photograph: an IOL lies in the vitreous cavity over the lower retina, which is tessellated.

blocks.p: An IOL can decentre or dislocate early, after capsule rupture. It can also dislocate years later inside its bag when the zonules fail, as in pseudoexfoliation or high myopia. The zonules are the fibres that hold the lens to the ciliary body. Symptoms are blurred or double vision and seeing the lens edge. Options include repositioning and fixation to the iris or sclera, or exchange. A lens in the vitreous needs vitrectomy.

blocks.pearl: Pain and falling vision in the first week after cataract surgery is endophthalmitis until proven otherwise. It needs same-day review, vitreous tap and intravitreal antibiotics (vancomycin and ceftazidime).

ul: Promising perfect vision to an eye with macular disease.
Missing pseudoexfoliation before surgery: weak zonules and a small pupil raise the risk.
Forgetting that a child with cataract needs amblyopia treatment after surgery.

notes.title: Proptosis (forward bulging of the eye): orbital cellulitis, thyroid eye disease (TED) or a mass
notes.sub: Separate preseptal from orbital, spot optic nerve threat, image well

blocks.p: Proptosis is forward displacement of the eye. Speed of onset and the patient's age point to the cause. Days suggest infection or inflammation. Weeks to months suggest TED or a tumour. A rapidly growing mass in a child is a malignancy until proven otherwise. Axial proptosis suggests a lesion inside the muscle cone. Displacement to one side suggests a mass outside it.

ul: Measure proptosis with an exophthalmometer. An asymmetry of more than 2 millimetres (mm) is significant.
Test visual acuity, colour vision and eye movements, and examine the optic disc in every patient. Check the pupils for a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD).
Look for lid retraction, lid lag, chemosis, a mass you can feel, and exposure of the cornea.

blocks.p: Preseptal cellulitis is confined to the lid. Orbital cellulitis lies behind the orbital septum (the fibrous sheet behind the lid). It shows proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, chemosis, reduced vision or an RAPD. It usually spreads from the ethmoid sinuses through the thin lamina papyracea, especially in children. The Chandler classification runs from preseptal cellulitis through orbital cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess and orbital abscess. It ends with cavernous sinus thrombosis.

ul: Admit, give intravenous antibiotics under local protocol, and involve ear, nose and throat (ENT) surgeons. Check vision and pupils regularly.

Arrange contrast computed tomography (CT) of the orbits and sinuses if there are orbital signs or vision cannot be assessed. Also scan if there is no improvement within 24 to 48 hours, or neurological signs appear.
Drain an abscess that is large or not responding, or that threatens the optic nerve. Optic nerve compression can cause permanent loss of vision in that eye.

blocks.p: TED is the commonest cause of proptosis in adults, one-sided or both. It enlarges the extraocular muscles, most often the inferior and medial rectus. The European Group on Graves' Orbitopathy (EUGOGO) 2021 guideline grades activity with the clinical activity score (CAS). It grades severity as mild, moderate-to-severe or sight-threatening. Everyone needs smoking cessation, stable thyroid function and lubrication. Selenium helps mild, recent disease. Active moderate-to-severe disease is treated with intravenous methylprednisolone, with mycophenolate. Second-line options include teprotumumab. **Dysthyroid optic neuropathy** is an emergency. Enlarged muscles crowd and compress the optic nerve at the orbital apex. This can cause permanent loss of vision in that eye. It needs high-dose intravenous steroid and, if needed, orbital decompression.

blocks.p: In adults, cavernous venous malformation and lymphoma are common. In children, dermoid cysts, capillary haemangioma and, urgently, rhabdomyosarcoma. Ultrasound shows shape and internal reflectivity. But CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) defines the extent, and many lesions need a biopsy.

blocks.pearl: In a swollen red eyelid, move the eye and check the pupil. Pain on movement, restriction or an RAPD makes it orbital. Orbital cellulitis means admission.

ul: Lid swelling in a child hides proptosis and restriction; open the lids and look.
Optic neuropathy in TED can occur in a quiet, barely proptosed eye.
Giving steroids before a biopsy can mask orbital lymphoma.
